text: And now that you don’t have to be perfect, you can be good.
author: John Steinbeck
citation: East of Eden (1952), Part 4, ch. 53, sec. 3

text:
‘Hope’ is the thing with feathers
That perches in the soul
And sings the tune without the words
And never stops at all
author: Emily Dickinson
citation: Fr314 / J254, first stanza (c. 1861)

text: I’m not afraid of storms, for I’m learning how to sail my ship.
author: Louisa May Alcott
citation: Little Women (1868), ch. 44 “My Lord and Lady”, spoken by Amy

text: Almost everything will work again if you unplug it for a few minutes, including you.
author: Anne Lamott
citation: “12 truths I learned from life and writing”, TED2017 (first posted on Facebook, 8 April 2015)

text: The best way out is always through.
author: Robert Frost
citation: “A Servant to Servants”, North of Boston (1914)

text: Learn, that the present hour alone is man’s.
author: Samuel Johnson
citation: The Tragedy of Irene (1749), Act III, Sc. 2

text: Hope is necessary in every condition.
author: Samuel Johnson
citation: The Rambler (1750–1752) · No. 67 (6 November 1750)

text: Pleasure is very seldom found where it is sought. Our brightest blazes of gladness are commonly kindled by unexpected sparks.
author: Samuel Johnson

text: Many things difficult to design prove easy to performance.
author: Samuel Johnson
work: The History of Rasselas, Prince of Abissinia
citation: The History of Rasselas, Prince of Abissinia (1759) · Ch. XXVI · Ch. ??{incorrect chapter}

text: The world is not yet exhausted: let me see something to-morrow which I never saw before.
author: Samuel Johnson
work: The History of Rasselas, Prince of Abissinia
citation: The History of Rasselas, Prince of Abissinia (1759) · Ch. XLVII

text: The remedy for weakness is not brooding over weakness, but thinking of strength. Teach men of strength that is already within them.
author: Swami Vivekananda
citation: Call to the Nation

text: A tremendous stream is flowing toward the ocean, carrying us all along with it; and though like straws and scraps of paper we may at times float aimlessly about, in the long run we are sure to join the Ocean of Life and Bliss.
author: Swami Vivekananda
citation: Pearls of Wisdom

text: Are great things ever done smoothly? Time, patience, and indomitable will must show.
author: Swami Vivekananda
citation: Pearls of Wisdom

text: Every step I take in light is mine forever.
author: Swami Vivekananda
citation: Pearls of Wisdom

text: I fervently wish no misery ever came near anyone; yet it is that alone that gives us an insight into the depths of our lives, does it not? In our moments of anguish, gates barred forever seem to open and let in many a flood of light.
author: Swami Vivekananda
citation: Pearls of Wisdom

text: The past was great no doubt, but I sincerely believe that the future will be more glorious still.
author: Swami Vivekananda
citation: Pearls of Wisdom

text: This life is a hard fact; work your way through it boldly, though it may be adamantine; no matter, the soul is stronger.
author: Swami Vivekananda
citation: Pearls of Wisdom

text: Work on with the intrepidity of a lion but at the same time with the tenderness of a flower.
author: Swami Vivekananda
citation: Pearls of Wisdom

text: We can make our minds so like still water that beings gather about us that they may see, it may be, their own images, and so live for a moment with a clearer, perhaps even with a fiercer life because of our quiet.
author: W. B. Yeats
citation: "Earth, Fire and Water" from The Celtic Twilight (1893)

text:
Time can but make it easier to be wise
Though now it seems impossible, and so
All that you need is patience.
author: W. B. Yeats
citation: In The Seven Woods (1904) · The Folly Of Being Comforted

text:
The trees are in their autumn beauty,
The woodland paths are dry,
Under the October twilight the water
Mirrors a still sky.
author: W. B. Yeats
citation: The Wild Swans at Coole (1919) · The Wild Swans At Coole, st. 1

text:
While on the shop and street I gazed
My body of a sudden blazed;
And twenty minutes more or less
It seemed, so great my happiness,
That I was blessed and could bless.
author: W. B. Yeats
citation: The Winding Stair and Other Poems (1933) · Vacillation · IV

text: O light! This is the cry of all the characters of ancient drama brought face to face with their fate. This last resort was ours, too, and I knew it now. In the middle of winter I at last discovered that there was in me an invincible summer.
author: Albert Camus
citation: Return to Tipasa (1954) · Variant translation: In the depths of winter, I finally learned that within me there lay an invincible summer.

text: Autumn is a second Spring when every leaf is a flower.
author: Albert Camus
citation: As quoted in Visions from Earth (2004) by James R. Miller, p. 126

text: It takes time to live. Like any work of art, life needs to be thought about.
author: Albert Camus
citation: A Happy Death (written 1936-38 (published in 1971, over 11 years after the author's death))

text: Blessed are the hearts that can bend; they shall never be broken.
author: Albert Camus
citation: A Happy Death (written 1936-38 (published in 1971, over 11 years after the author's death))

text: Maman used to say that you can always find something to be happy about.
author: Albert Camus
citation: The Stranger (1942)

text: Everything considered, a determined soul will always manage.
author: Albert Camus
citation: The Myth of Sisyphus (1942) · An Absurd Reasoning

text: There are more things to admire in men than to despise.
author: Albert Camus
citation: The Plague (1947) · V.5 (tr. Stuart Gilbert, 1948)

text: Let’s not beat around the bush; I love life — that’s my real weakness. I love it so much that I am incapable of imagining what is not life.
author: Albert Camus
citation: The Fall (1956)

text:
I ask myself: are defeats necessary?
Well, necessary or not, they happen. When we first begin fighting for a dream, we have no experience and make mistakes. The secret of life, though, is to fall seven times and to get up eight times.
author: Paulo Coelho
citation: The Alchemist (1988) · Introduction, p. xi.

text: It is said that the darkest hour of the night comes just before the dawn.
author: Paulo Coelho
citation: The Alchemist (1988) · p. 132.

text: Warriors of the light are not perfect. Their beauty lies in accepting this fact and still desiring to grow and to learn.
author: Paulo Coelho
work: The Manual of the Warrior of Light
citation: The Manual of the Warrior of Light (1997)

text: Laugh at your worries and insecurities. View your anxieties with humor. It will be difficult at first, but you’ll gradually get used to it.
author: Paulo Coelho
citation: The Witch of Portobello (2007) · p. 152.

text: If I had to give you one piece of advice, it would be this: don’t be intimidated by other people’s opinions.
author: Paulo Coelho
citation: Aleph (2011)

text: Love is the only thing that will save us, independent of any mistakes we may make. Love is always stronger.
author: Paulo Coelho
citation: Aleph (2011)

text: In the cycle of nature there is no such thing as victory or defeat; there is only movement. The winter struggles to reign supreme, but in the end is obliged to accept spring’s victory, which brings with it flowers and happiness.
author: Paulo Coelho
citation: Manuscript Found in Accra (2012)

text: Sometimes, when loneliness seems about to crush everything, the only way to resist is to keep on loving.
author: Paulo Coelho
citation: Manuscript Found in Accra (2012)

text: No one can go back, but everyone can go forward. And tomorrow, when the sun rises, all you have to say to yourselves is: I am going to think of this day as the first day of my life.
author: Paulo Coelho
citation: Manuscript Found in Accra (2012)

text: And if I’m alone in bed, I will go over to window, look up at the sky and feel certain that loneliness is a lie, because the Universe is there to keep me company.
author: Paulo Coelho
citation: Manuscript Found in Accra (2012)

text: Let us forget all that we are taught about how it is noble to give and humiliating to receive. Because for most people, generosity consists only in giving, but receiving is also an act of love. Allowing someone else to make us happy will make them happy too.
author: Paulo Coelho
citation: Manuscript Found in Accra (2012)

text: In ancient times cats were worshiped as gods; they have not forgotten this.
author: Terry Pratchett
work: Ghost Cats: Human Encounters with Feline Spirits
citation: General sources · Pratchett is credited as author of this, as quoted in Ghost Cats : Human Encounters with Feline Spirits (2007) by Dusty Rainbolt, p. 7, and in Chicken Soup for the Soul : What I Learned from the Cat (2009) by Jack Canfield, Mark Victor Hansen, and Amy Newmark · Variant: In ancient times, cats were worshiped as gods. They have never forgotten this.

text: Nothing has to happen. History isn’t something you live. It is something you make. One decision. One person. At the right time. Nothing is too small to make a difference. Anything can be changed.
author: Terry Pratchett
citation: The Carpet People (1971; 1992) · Chapter 13 (p. 120)

text: Everything makes sense a bit at a time. But when you try to think of it all at once, it comes out wrong.
author: Terry Pratchett
citation: Only You Can Save Mankind (1992)

text: Love is not consolation, it is light.
author: Simone Weil
citation: As quoted in Simone Weil (1954) by Eric Walter Frederick Tomlin, p. 47

text: God’s love for us is not the reason for which we should love him. God’s love for us is the reason for us to love ourselves.
author: Simone Weil
citation: Simone Weil : An Anthology (1986) · Love (1947) · p. 270

text: Your pain is the breaking of the shell that encloses your understanding. Even as the stone of the fruit must break, that its heart may stand in the sun, so must you know pain.
author: Kahlil Gibran
citation: The Prophet (1923)

text: A sense of humour is a sense of proportion.
author: Kahlil Gibran
citation: Sand and Foam (1926)

text: Solitude is a silent storm that breaks down all our dead branches; Yet it sends our living roots deeper into the living heart of the living earth.
author: Kahlil Gibran
citation: Sand and Foam (1926)

text:
I sorrowed no more.
Who would sorrow for a sea that is unveiling its face, or for a mountain that laughs in the sun?
author: Kahlil Gibran
citation: Jesus, The Son of Man (1928) · Philip: And When He Died All Mankind Died

text: How amazing time is, and how amazing we are.
author: Kahlil Gibran
work: The Vision: Reflections on the Way of the Soul
citation: The Vision: Reflections on the Way of the Soul (1994) · Children of Gods, Scions of Apes

text: Our Creator would never have made such lovely days, and have given us the deep hearts to enjoy them, above and beyond all thought, unless we were meant to be immortal.
author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
citation: "The Old Manse": The Author Makes the Reader Acquainted with His Abode from Mosses from an Old Manse (1846)

text: Every individual has a place to fill in the world, and is important, in some respect, whether he chooses to be so or not.
author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
citation: Notebooks · The American Notebooks (1835 - 1853) · 1836

text: What would a man do, if he were compelled to live always in the sultry heat of society, and could never bathe himself in cool solitude?
author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
citation: Notebooks · The American Notebooks (1835 - 1853) · 1836

text: I cannot endure to waste anything so precious as autumnal sunshine by staying in the house.
author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
citation: Notebooks · The American Notebooks (1835 - 1853) · 1842

text: Love, whether newly born, or aroused from a deathlike slumber, must always create sunshine, filling the heart so full of radiance, that it overflows upon the outward world.
author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
citation: The Scarlet Letter (1850) · Chapter XVIII: A Flood of Sunshine

text: Romance and poetry, ivy, lichens and wallflowers need ruin to make them grow.
author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
citation: The Marble Faun (1860) · Preface

text: There is really no such thing as bad weather, only different kinds of good weather.
author: John Ruskin
citation: Quoted by John Lubbock, 1st Baron Avebury, The Use of Life, chapter IV: "Recreation" (1894)

text: Remember that the most beautiful things in the world are the most useless: peacocks and lilies, for instance.
author: John Ruskin
citation: The Stones of Venice (1853) · Volume I, chapter II, section 17

text: Endurance is nobler than strength, and patience than beauty.
author: John Ruskin
citation: The Two Paths (1859) · Lecture IV: The Influence of Imagination in Architecture, section 137

text: All you have really to do is to keep your back as straight as you can; and not think about what is upon it. The real and essential meaning of “virtue” is that straightness of back.
author: John Ruskin
citation: The Ethics of the Dust (1875) · Lecture VII: Home Virtues, section 80

text: I never lose an opportunity of urging a practical beginning, however small, for it is wonderful how often in such matters the mustard-seed germinates and roots itself.
author: Florence Nightingale
citation: Letter to a friend, quoted in The Life of Florence Nightingale Vol. II (1914) by Edward Tyas Cook, p. 406

text: To have faith is to trust yourself to the water. When you swim you don’t grab hold of the water, because if you do you will sink and drown. Instead you relax, and float.
author: Alan Watts
citation: The Essence of Alan Watts (1977)

text: This is the real secret of life—to be completely engaged with what you are doing in the here and now. And instead of calling it work, realize it is play.
author: Alan Watts
citation: The Essence of Alan Watts (1977)

text: There is nothing wrong with meditating just to meditate, in the same way that you listen to music just for the music. If you go to concerts to “get culture” or to improve your mind, you will sit there as deaf as a doorpost.
author: Alan Watts
citation: The Book on the Taboo Against Knowing Who You Are (1966) · p. 90

text: Life and love generate effort, but effort will not generate them.
author: Alan Watts
citation: The Book on the Taboo Against Knowing Who You Are (1966) · p. 56

text: A person who thinks all the time has nothing to think about except thoughts. So he loses touch with reality, and lives in a world of illusion.
author: Alan Watts
citation: Alan Watts Teaches Meditation (1992)

text: Every one of us is marvellous and complicated and interesting and gorgeous just as we are.
author: Alan Watts
citation: Out of Your Mind: Tricksters, Interdependence, and the Cosmic Game of Hide-and-Seek (2017) · p. 42

text:
The present moment
contains past and future.
The secret of transformation,
is in the way we handle this very moment.
author: Thich Nhat Hanh
citation: Understanding Our Mind (2006) Parallax Press

text: If in our daily life we can smile, if we can be peaceful and happy, not only we, but everyone will profit from it.
author: Thich Nhat Hanh
citation: Peace Is Every Step : The Path of Mindfulness in Everyday Life (1992) Bantam reissue

text: The miracle is not to walk on water. The miracle is to walk on the green earth in the present moment, to appreciate the peace and beauty that are available now.
author: Thich Nhat Hanh
citation: Touching Peace (1992), p. 1. Parallax Press

text: Drink your tea slowly and reverently, as if it is the axis on which the whole earth revolves—slowly, evenly, without rushing toward the future. Live the actual moment. Only this actual moment is life.
author: Thich Nhat Hanh
citation: The Miracle of Mindfulness (1999)

text: It’s wonderful to be alive and to walk on earth.
author: Thich Nhat Hanh
citation: Talk at Stonehill College (2002)

text: You are a miracle, and everything you touch could be a miracle.
author: Thich Nhat Hanh
citation: Episode of the National Public Radio program Speaking of Faith : "Brother Thay: A Radio Pilgrimage with Thich Nhat Hanh" (2003)

text: We have more possibilities available in each moment than we realize.
author: Thich Nhat Hanh
citation: As quoted in Visions from Earth (2004) by James Miller

text: Your true home is in the here and the now. It is not limited by time, space, nationality, or race.
author: Thich Nhat Hanh
citation: "Returning Home", Shambhala Sun (March 2006)

text: Life is filled with suffering, but it is also filled with many wonders, such as the blue sky, the sunshine, and the eyes of a baby. To suffer is not enough. We must also be in touch with the wonders of life. They are within us and all around us, everywhere, anytime.
author: Thich Nhat Hanh
citation: Being Peace (1987)

text: Real strength is not in power, money, or weapons, but in deep, inner peace. If we change our daily lives—the way we think, speak, and act—we change the world. The best way to take care of the environment is to take care of the environmentalist.
author: Thich Nhat Hanh
citation: The Sun My Heart (1996)

text: Breath is the bridge which connects life to consciousness, which unites your body to your thoughts. Whenever your mind becomes scattered, use your breath as the means to take hold of your mind again.
author: Thich Nhat Hanh
citation: The Miracle of Mindfulness: An Introduction to the Practice of Meditation (1999) · Page 15

text: I don’t know who I am / but you know, life is for learning.
author: Joni Mitchell
citation: Song lyrics · "Woodstock"

text:
We are stardust,
We are golden,
And we’ve got to get ourselves
Back to the garden.
author: Joni Mitchell
citation: Song lyrics · "Woodstock"

text:
I wanna be strong,
I wanna laugh along,
I wanna belong to the living.
Alive, alive, I wanna get up and jive,
Wanna wreck my stockings in some jukebox dive.
author: Joni Mitchell
citation: Song lyrics · "All I Want" from Blue

text: Laughing and crying, you know it’s the same release.
author: Joni Mitchell
citation: Song lyrics · "People's Parties"

text: Open, honest, truth-telling individuals value privacy. We all need spaces where we can be alone with thoughts and feelings - where we can experience healthy psychological autonomy and can choose to share when we want to.
author: bell hooks
citation: Miscellaneous · All About Love: New Visions (2000)

text: We must be willing to get rid of the life we’ve planned, so as to have the life that is waiting for us.
author: Joseph Campbell
citation: A Joseph Campbell Companion: Reflections on the Art of Living (1991), p. 18

text: Find a place where there’s joy, and the joy will burn out the pain.
author: Joseph Campbell
citation: A Joseph Campbell Companion: Reflections on the Art of Living (1991), p. 152

text: One thing that comes out in myths is that at the bottom of the abyss comes the voice of salvation. The black moment is the moment when the real message of transformation is going to come. At the darkest moment comes the light.
author: Joseph Campbell
citation: The Power of Myth (book) · Ch. 2 : The Journey Inward

text: I say, follow your bliss and don’t be afraid, and doors will open where you didn’t know they were going to be.
author: Joseph Campbell
citation: The Power of Myth (book) · p. 120

text:
When I was One,
I had just begun.
When I was Two,
I was nearly new.
When I was Three
I was hardly me.
When I was Four,
I was not much more.
When I was Five,
I was just alive.
But now I am Six,
I’m as clever as clever,
So I think I’ll be six now for ever and ever.
author: A. A. Milne
citation: Now We Are Six (1927) · The End.

text:
“I don’t see much sense in that,” said Rabbit.
“No,” said Pooh humbly, “there isn’t. But there was going to be when I began it. It’s just that something happened to it on the way.”
author: A. A. Milne
citation: The House at Pooh Corner (1928) · Chapter Seven.

text: “You only blinched inside,” said Pooh, “and that’s the bravest way for a Very Small Animal not to blinch that there is.”
author: A. A. Milne
citation: The House at Pooh Corner (1928) · Chapter Ten.

text: “They wanted to come in after the pounds”, explained Pooh, “so I let them. It’s the best way to write poetry, letting things come”.
author: A. A. Milne
citation: The House at Pooh Corner (1928)

text: Nature is satisfied with little; and if she is, I am also.
author: Baruch Spinoza
citation: As quoted in The Story of Philosophy (1933) by Will Durant, p. 176

text: But I believe without any doubt at all that our greatest good fortune was that even in the most extreme difficulties we might lose our patience but never our sense of humor.
author: Gabriel García Márquez
citation: Living to Tell the Tale (2002)

text: I’ll have to calm down a bit. Or else I’ll burst with happiness.
author: Tove Jansson
citation: "Moominsummer Madness" (The Moomins, #5)

text: A person can find anything if he takes the time, that is, if he can afford to look. And while he’s looking, he’s free, and he finds things he never expected.
author: Tove Jansson
citation: Sommarboken (A Summer Book) (1972).

text: I only want to live in peace, plant potatoes and dream!
author: Tove Jansson
citation: "Moomin: The Complete Tove Jansson Comic Strip, Vol. 1" (1977).

text: We are all in the gutter, but some of us are looking at the stars.
author: Oscar Wilde
citation: Lady Windermere's Fan (1892) · Lord Darlington, Act III

text: Experience is the name everyone gives to their mistakes.
author: Oscar Wilde
citation: Lady Windermere's Fan (1892) · Mr. Dumby, Act III · First used by Wilde in Vera; or, The Nihilists

text: To love oneself is the beginning of a life-long romance.
author: Oscar Wilde
citation: Phrases and Philosophies for the Use of the Young (1894)

text: If you are not too long, I will wait here for you all my life.
author: Oscar Wilde
citation: The Importance of Being Earnest (1895) · Gwendolen, Act III

text: It seems to me that we all look at Nature too much, and live with her too little.
author: Oscar Wilde
citation: De Profundis (1897)

text: Where there is sorrow there is holy ground.
author: Oscar Wilde
citation: De Profundis (1897)

text: The weakest living creature, by concentrating his powers on a single object, can accomplish something.
author: Thomas Carlyle
citation: The life of Friedrich Schiller: Comprehending an examination of his works (1825).

text: When the oak-tree is felled, the whole forest echoes with it; but a hundred acorns are planted silently by some unnoticed breeze.
author: Thomas Carlyle
citation: Critical and Miscellaneous Essays (1827–1855) · On History.

text: Our grand business undoubtedly is, not to see what lies dimly at a distance, but to do what lies clearly at hand.
author: Thomas Carlyle
citation: Signs of the Times (1829)

text: “Do the Duty which lies nearest thee,” which thou knowest to be a Duty! Thy second Duty will already have become clearer.
author: Thomas Carlyle
citation: Sartor Resartus (1833–1834) · Bk. II, ch. 9.

text: Under all speech that is good for anything there lies a silence that is better. Silence is deep as Eternity; speech is shallow as Time.
author: Thomas Carlyle
citation: Sir Walter Scott (1838)

text: Nothing that was worthy in the past departs; no truth or goodness realized by man ever dies, or can die.
author: Thomas Carlyle
citation: Sir Walter Scott (1838)

text: Every noble work is at first impossible.
author: Thomas Carlyle
citation: Past and Present (1843) · From Past and Present (1843), Chapter XI : Labour

text: It is the very joy of man’s heart to admire, where he can; nothing so lifts him from all his mean imprisonments, were it but for moments, as true admiration.
author: Thomas Carlyle
citation: Past and Present (1843)

text:
All silence is.
All emptiness.
And now:
The dawn.
author: Ray Bradbury
citation: "Emily Dickinson, where are you? Herman Melville called your name last night in his sleep!" in When Elephants Last In The Dooryard Bloomed : Celebrations For Almost Any Day In The Year (1973)

text: We are the miracle of force and matter making itself over into imagination and will. Incredible. The Life Force experimenting with forms. You for one. Me for another. The Universe has shouted itself alive. We are one of the shouts.
author: Ray Bradbury
work: I Sing the Body Electric: And Other Stories
citation: "G. B. S. — Mark V", in I Sing the Body Electric: And Other Stories (1998)

text: If you’re reluctant to weep, you won’t live a full and complete life.
author: Ray Bradbury
citation: Personal lessons from futurist Ray Bradbury on crying, escaping, laughing, by Mick Mortlock; Oregon Live (6 June 2012)

text: The sun did not rise, it overflowed.
author: Ray Bradbury
citation: Dandelion Wine (1957) · p. 211

text: God, how we get our fingers in each other’s clay. That’s friendship, each playing the potter to see what shapes we can make of the other.
author: Ray Bradbury
citation: Something Wicked This Way Comes (1962) · Chapter 3 (p. 18)

text: Night had come on like the closing of a great but gentle eye.
author: Ray Bradbury
citation: R Is for Rocket (1962) · Here There Be Tygers (1951)

text:
Leave off losings, and take on winnings, Erase all mortal ends, give birth to only new beginnings,
In a billion years of morning and a billion years of sleep.
author: Ray Bradbury
citation: Christ, Old Student in a New School (1972)

text: That’s the whole secret: to do things that excite you.
author: Ray Bradbury
citation: The Paris Review interview (2010)

text: I don’t understand writers who have to work at it. I like to play. I’m interested in having fun with ideas, throwing them up in the air like confetti and then running under them.
author: Ray Bradbury
citation: The Paris Review interview (2010)

text:
And the song, from beginning to end,
I found again in the heart of a friend.
author: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
citation: The Arrow and the Song, st. 3.

text:
Far off I hear the crowing of the cocks,
And through the opening door that time unlocks
Feel the fresh breathing of To-morrow creep.
author: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
citation: "To-morrow", in The Atlantic Monthly, vol. 17, no. 103 (May 1866), p. 552

author: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
citation: The Bells of San Blas, st. 11 (March 15, 1882).

text:
Oh, fear not in a world like this,
And thou shalt know erelong,—
Know how sublime a thing it is
To suffer and be strong.
author: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
citation: Voices of the Night (1839) · The Light of Stars, st. 9.

text: Believe me, every heart has its secret sorrows, which the world knows not, and oftentimes we call a man cold, when he is only sad.
author: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
citation: Hyperion (1839) · Bk. III, Ch. 4.

author: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
citation: Ballads and Other Poems (1842) · The Rainy Day, originally in Bentley's Miscellany (Dec. 1841) p. 626

text:
And the night shall be filled with music,
And the cares, that infest the day,
Shall fold their tents, like the Arabs,
And as silently steal away.
author: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
citation: The Belfry of Bruges and Other Poems (1845) · The Day is Done · St. 11.

text:
Silently one by one, in the infinite meadows of heaven,
Blossomed the lovely stars, the forget-me-nots of the angels.
author: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
citation: Evangeline: A Tale of Acadie (1847) · Part I, section 3.

author: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
citation: Evangeline: A Tale of Acadie (1847) · Part II, section 1.

text: If spring came but once in a century, instead of once a year, or burst forth with the sound of an earthquake, and not in silence, what wonder and expectation there would be in all hearts to behold the miraculous change!
author: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
citation: Kavanagh: A Tale (1849) · Chapter 13.

text: Give what you have. To someone, it may be better than you dare to think.
author: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
citation: Kavanagh: A Tale (1849) · Chapter 30.

author: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
citation: The Seaside and the Fireside (1850) · The Builders, st. 2.

text: All things come round to him who will but wait.
author: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
work: The Student’s Tale: The Falcon of Ser Federigo
citation: Tales of a Wayside Inn (1863–1874) · Pt. I, The Student's Tale: The Falcon of Ser Federigo, last line.

text:
For age is opportunity no less
Than youth itself, though in another dress,
And as the evening twilight fades away
The sky is filled with stars, invisible by day.
author: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
citation: Morituri Salutamus (1875) · St. 25.

author: Mahatma Gandhi

author: Mark Twain

author: Mark Twain

text: One of the brightest gems in the New England weather is the dazzling uncertainty of it.
author: Mark Twain
citation: New England Weather, speech to the New England Society (December 22, 1876)

text: Nothing that grieves us can be called little: by the eternal laws of proportion a child’s loss of a doll and a king’s loss of a crown are events of the same size.
author: Mark Twain
citation: "Which was the Dream?" (1898)

text: I have seen the truth; I have seen and I know that people can be beautiful and happy without losing the power of living on earth. I will not and cannot believe that evil is the normal condition of mankind. And it is just this faith of mine that they laugh at.
author: Fyodor Dostoyevsky

author: Fyodor Dostoyevsky

author: Thomas à Kempis

text: First keep the peace within yourself, then you can also bring peace to others.
author: Thomas à Kempis

text: No need to hurry. No need to sparkle. No need to be anybody but oneself.
author: Virginia Woolf
citation: A Room of One's Own (1929) · Ch. 1, p. 17

text: I had a very pleasant evening, however, though you will probably find out that there was no particular reason for it; but I do not think it worth while to wait for enjoyment until there is some real opportunity for it.
author: Jane Austen
work: Letters of Jane Austen — Brabourne Edition
citation: Letters · Letter (1799-01-21) [Letters of Jane Austen -- Brabourne Edition]

text: The pleasures of friendship, of unreserved conversation, of similarity of taste and opinions will make good amends for orange wine.
author: Jane Austen
work: Letters of Jane Austen — Brabourne Edition
citation: Letters · Letter to Cassandra (1808-06-20) [Letters of Jane Austen -- Brabourne Edition]

text: Ah! there is nothing like staying at home for real comfort.
author: Jane Austen
citation: Works · Emma (1815)

text: They say the first sentence in any speech is always the hardest. Well, that one’s behind me, anyway.
author: Wisława Szymborska
citation: The Poet and the World (1996)

text: Whatever inspiration is, it’s born from a continuous “I don’t know.”
author: Wisława Szymborska
citation: The Poet and the World (1996)

text:
I’m working on the world,
revised, improved edition,
featuring fun for fools
blues for brooders,
combs for bald pates,
tricks for old dogs.
author: Wisława Szymborska
citation: Poems New and Collected (1998) · Calling Out to Yeti (1957) · I'm Working on the World"

text: We have been troubled about the world, and had almost lost faith in man; it helps to think about the long history of the earth, and of how life came to be. And when we think in terms of millions of years, we are not so impatient that our own problems be solved tomorrow.
author: Rachel Carson
citation: Speech accepting the John Burroughs Medal (April 1952); also in Lost Woods: The Discovered Writing of Rachel Carson (1999) edited by Linda Lear, p. 96

text: A rainy day is the perfect time for a walk in the woods.
author: Rachel Carson
citation: The Sense of Wonder (1965)

text: Those who dwell, as scientists or laymen, among the beauties and mysteries of the earth are never alone or weary of life.
author: Rachel Carson
citation: The Sense of Wonder (1965)

text: Those who contemplate the beauty of the earth find reserves of strength that will endure as long as life lasts.
author: Rachel Carson
citation: The Sense of Wonder (1965)

text: Reflect upon your present blessings — of which every man has many — not on your past misfortunes, of which all men have some.
author: Charles Dickens
citation: Sketches by Boz (1836-1837) · Characters, Ch. 2: A Christmas Dinner

text: Suffering has been stronger than all other teaching, and has taught me to understand what your heart used to be. I have been bent and broken, but — I hope — into a better shape.
author: Charles Dickens
citation: Great Expectations (1860-1861) · Ch. 59

text: There is nothing either good or bad, but thinking makes it so.
author: William Shakespeare
citation: William Shakespeare Quotes · Hamlet (1600–1) · Hamlet, Act II, scene ii.

text:
Come what come may,
Time and the hour runs through the roughest day.
author: William Shakespeare
citation: William Shakespeare Quotes · Macbeth (1606) · Macbeth, Act I, scene iii.

text: When I get sick of what men do, I have only to walk a few steps in another direction to see what spiders do. Or what the weather does. This sustains me very well indeed.
author: E. B. White
citation: Letter to Carrie A. Wilson (1 May 1951)

text: If the world were merely seductive, that would be easy. If it were merely challenging, that would be no problem. But I arise in the morning torn between a desire to improve (or save) the world and a desire to enjoy (or savor) the world. This makes it hard to plan the day.
author: E. B. White
citation: Quoted in profile by Israel Shenker, "E. B. White: Notes and Comment by Author", The New York Times (11 July 1969)

text: Life’s meaning has always eluded me and I guess it always will. But I love it just the same.
author: E. B. White
citation: Letter to Mary Virginia Parrish (29 August 1969)

text: As long as there is one upright man, as long as there is one compassionate woman, the contagion may spread and the scene is not desolate. Hope is the one thing left to us in a bad time.
author: E. B. White
citation: Letter to M. Nadeau (30 March 1973)

text: Sailors have an expression about the weather: they say the weather is a great bluffer. I guess the same is true of our human society — things can look dark, then a break shows in the clouds, and all is changed.
author: E. B. White
citation: Letter to M. Nadeau (30 March 1973)

text: Life is always a rich and steady time when you are waiting for something to happen or to hatch.
author: E. B. White
citation: Charlotte's Web (1952) · Ch. 22

text:
It is brave to be involved
To be not fearful to be unresolved.
author: Gwendolyn Brooks
citation: "do not be afraid of no" from Annie Allen (1949)

text:
To be in love
Is to touch with a lighter hand.
In yourself you stretch, you are well.
author: Gwendolyn Brooks
citation: "To Be In Love"

text:
I pass you my Poem! — to tell you
we are all vulnerable —
the midget, the Mighty,
the richest, the poor.
Men, women, children, and trees.
I am vulnerable.
author: Gwendolyn Brooks
citation: Winnie (1988) · "Song of Winnie"

text: My Poem is life, and not finished.
author: Gwendolyn Brooks
citation: Winnie (1988) · "Song of Winnie"

text:
Wherever life can grow, it will.
It will sprout out,
and do the best it can.
author: Gwendolyn Brooks
citation: Winnie (1988) · "Song of Winnie"

text: You don’t get all your questions answered in this world.
author: Gwendolyn Brooks
citation: Winnie (1988) · "Song of Winnie"

text: Nothing is more common than good things: the point in question is only to discriminate them; and it is certain that they are all natural and within our reach and even known to all mankind.
author: Blaise Pascal
citation: The Art of Persuasion

text: I have learned that success is to be measured not so much by the position that one has reached in life as by the obstacles which he has overcome while trying to succeed.
author: Booker T. Washington
citation: 1900s · Up From Slavery (1901) · Chapter II: Boyhood Days

text: In anything at all, perfection is finally attained not when there is no longer anything to add, but when there is no longer anything to take away, when a body has been stripped down to its nakedness.
author: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry
citation: Terre des Hommes (1939) · Ch III : The Tool · It seems that perfection is attained not when there is nothing more to add, but when there is nothing more to remove.

text: There are years that ask questions and years that answer.
author: Zora Neale Hurston

author: Zora Neale Hurston

text: What a comfort one familiar face is in a howling wilderness of strangers!
author: L. M. Montgomery

text: It is never quite safe to think we have done with life. When we imagine we have finished our story fate has a trick of turning the page and showing us yet another chapter.
author: L. M. Montgomery

text: We miss so much out of life if we don’t love. The more we love the richer life is—even if it is only some little furry or feathery pet.
author: L. M. Montgomery
citation: Rainbow Valley (1919)

text: What is a weed? A plant whose virtues have yet to be discovered.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: Fortune of the Republic (1878)

text: We are never without a pilot. When we know not how to steer, and dare not hoist a sail, we can drift. The current knows the way, though we do not. The ship of heaven guides itself, and will not accept a wooden rudder.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: "The Sovereignty of Ethics", in The North America Review, no. 262 (May–June 1878) p. 407

text: Do not be too timid and squeamish about your actions. All life is an experiment. The more experiments you make the better.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: Journals (1822–1863) · November 11, 1842

text: The sky is the daily bread of the eyes.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

text: The stars awaken a certain reverence, because though always present, they are inaccessible; but all natural objects make a kindred impression, when the mind is open to their influence. Nature never wears a mean appearance.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: Nature (1836) · Nature

text:
But all sorts of things and weather
Must be taken in together
To make up a year,
And a sphere.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: Poems (1847) · Fable

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: Poems (1847) · Fable

text:
Rhodora! if the sages ask thee why
This charm is wasted on the earth and sky,
Tell them, dear, that, if eyes were made for seeing,
Then beauty is its own excuse for Being.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: Poems (1847) · The Rhodora

text: Keep cool: it will be all one a hundred years hence.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

text: All the great speakers were bad speakers at first.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

The music that can deepest reach,
And cure all ill, is cordial speech.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: May-Day and Other Pieces (1867) · Merlin's Song, II

Some of your hurts you have cured,
And the sharpest you still have survived,
But what torments of grief you endured
From evils which never arrived!
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

author: G. K. Chesterton

author: G. K. Chesterton

author: Henry David Thoreau

author: Henry David Thoreau

author: Henry David Thoreau

author: Robert Louis Stevenson

author: Robert Louis Stevenson

author: Robert Louis Stevenson
citation: The Silverado Squatters (1883) · Toils And Pleasures.

text:
The world is so full of a number of things,
I’m sure we should all be as happy as kings.
author: Robert Louis Stevenson

Go, little book, and wish to all
Flowers in the garden, meat in the hall,
A bin of wine, a spice of wit,
A house with lawns enclosing it,
A living river by the door,
A nightingale in the sycamore!
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
citation: Underwoods (1887) · Bk. I, Envoy · :Cf. Chaucer, Troilus and Cressida, bk. V, l. 1786

Wealth I ask not, hope nor love,
Nor a friend to know me;
All I ask, the heaven above
And the road below me.
author: Robert Louis Stevenson

I will make you brooches and toys for your delight
Of bird-song at morning and star-shine at night.
author: Robert Louis Stevenson

author: Robert Louis Stevenson

text: We are at the very beginning of time for the human race. It is not unreasonable that we grapple with problems. But there are tens of thousands of years in the future. Our responsibility is to do what we can, learn what we can, improve the solutions, and pass them on.
author: Richard Feynman

text: Some people say, “How can you live without knowing?” I do not know what they mean. I always live without knowing. That is easy. How you get to know is what I want to know.
author: Richard Feynman

text: The fact that you are not sure means that it is possible that there is another way someday.
author: Richard Feynman

text:

And carried aloft on the wings of the breeze;
For above and around me the wild wind is roaring,
Arousing to rapture the earth and the seas.
author: Anne Brontë

author: Anne Brontë

author: Søren Kierkegaard

text:
Happy the man whose wish and care
A few paternal acres bound,
Content to breathe his native air
In his own ground.
author: Alexander Pope

text: Just because we don’t understand doesn’t mean that the explanation doesn’t exist.
author: Madeleine L'Engle

text: The concentration of a small child at play is analogous to the concentration of the artist of any discipline. In real play, which is real concentration, the child is not only outside time, he is outside himself.
author: Madeleine L'Engle
citation: The Crosswicks Journal · A Circle of Quiet (1972) · Section 1.3

text: A self is not something static, tied up in a pretty parcel and handed to the child, finished and complete. A self is always becoming.
author: Madeleine L'Engle
citation: The Crosswicks Journal · A Circle of Quiet (1972) · Section 1.10

text: I wish that we worried more about asking the right questions instead of being so hung up on finding answers.
author: Madeleine L'Engle
citation: The Crosswicks Journal · A Circle of Quiet (1972) · Section 4.8

text: We are just an advanced breed of monkeys on a minor planet of a very average star. But we can understand the Universe. That makes us something very special.
author: Stephen Hawking
citation: Der Spiegel (17 October 1988)

text: Life would be tragic if it weren’t funny.
author: Stephen Hawking
citation: As quoted in "The Science of Second-Guessing", The New York Times (12 December 2004)

text: My expectations were reduced to zero when I was 21. Everything since then has been a bonus.
author: Stephen Hawking
citation: As quoted in "The Science of Second-Guessing", The New York Times (12 December 2004) · Unsourced variant: "When one's expectations are reduced to zero, one really appreciates everything one does have."

text: Black holes ain’t as black as they are painted. They are not the eternal prisons they were once thought. Things can get out of a black hole, both to the outside, and possibly to another universe. So if you feel you are in a black hole, don’t give up. There’s a way out.
author: Stephen Hawking
citation: Reith Lecture 2 : Black holes ain’t as black as they are painted (2015) · BBC Radio 4 audio file

text: So next time someone complains that you have made a mistake, tell him that may be a good thing. Because without imperfection, neither you nor I would exist.
author: Stephen Hawking
work: Into The Universe with Stephen Hawking

text: We are all different — but we share the same human spirit. Perhaps it’s human nature that we adapt — and survive.
author: Stephen Hawking
citation: Hawking (2013) · Official Trailer

text: The quest for certainty blocks the search for meaning. Uncertainty is the very condition to impel man to unfold his powers.
author: Erich Fromm

text: To the question whether I am a pessimist or an optimist, I answer that my knowledge is pessimistic, but my willing and hoping are optimistic.
author: Albert Schweitzer

citation: Out of My Life and Thought : An Autobiography (1933) · Epilogue, p. 242

text: Not one of us knows what effect his life produces, and what he gives to others; that is hidden from us and must remain so, though we are often allowed to see some little fraction of it, so that we may not lose courage.
author: Albert Schweitzer
citation: The Spiritual Life (1947) · p. 164

text: Fear is inevitable, I have to accept that, but I cannot allow it to paralyze me.
author: Isabel Allende

text: Any mind that is capable of a real sorrow is capable of good.
author: Harriet Beecher Stowe

author: J. R. R. Tolkien

text: Even as a kid, I felt isolated. Isolation makes you sensitive. As a kid, I felt I was the only person who was like that. But there’s a good side to isolation. It makes you sensitive, and sensitivity is part of the creative process.
author: Jim Henson

text: There’s great value in being able to step back and laugh at yourself, at life and at attitudes. Laughter helps you put everything into perspective.
author: Jim Henson

text: When you trick people into laughing at themselves, that’s wit. If you don’t laugh at yourself, everything becomes heavy.
author: Jim Henson
citation: Interview with The Boston Globe (1989)

text: No experience has been too unimportant, and the smallest event unfolds like a fate, and fate itself is like a wonderful, wide fabric in which every thread is guided by an infinitely tender hand and laid alongside another thread and is held and supported by a hundred others.
author: Rainer Maria Rilke
citation: Letters to a Young Poet (1934) · Letter Three (23 April 1903)

text: By health I mean the power to live a full, adult, living, breathing life in close contact with what I love — the earth and the wonders thereof — the sea — the sun.
author: Katherine Mansfield
citation: Entry in her journal (10 October 1922) which she tore out to send to John Middleton Murry, before changing her mind. This later became the last published entry in The Journal of Katherine Mansfield (1927) ed. J. Middleton Murry

text: I feel happy — deep down. All is well.
author: Katherine Mansfield
citation: Entry in her journal (10 October 1922) which she tore out to send to John Middleton Murry, before changing her mind. This later became the last published entry in The Journal of Katherine Mansfield (1927) edited by J. Middleton Murry

text: When we can begin to take our failures nonseriously, it means we are ceasing to be afraid of them. It is of immense importance to learn to laugh at ourselves.
author: Katherine Mansfield
citation: Journal entry (October 1922), published in The Journal of Katherine Mansfield (1927)

text: I always felt that the great high privilege, relief and comfort of friendship was that one had to explain nothing.
author: Katherine Mansfield
citation: As quoted in Katherine Mansfield : A Biography (1953) by Antony Alpers, p. 266

text: Love is our true destiny. We do not find the meaning of life by ourselves alone — we find it with another.
author: Thomas Merton
citation: Love and Living (1979) Part One : Love and Living, p. 27

text: We are not meant to resolve all contradictions but to live with them and rise above them and see them in the light of exterior and objective values which make them trivial by comparison.
author: Thomas Merton
citation: Thoughts in Solitude (1956)

text: Being alive is the Magic—being strong is the Magic.
author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
citation: The Secret Garden (1911) · Chapter 22

text: You know, I think everybody longs to be loved, and longs to know that he or she is lovable. And, consequently, the greatest thing that we can do is to help somebody know that they’re loved and capable of loving.
author: Fred Rogers
citation: Fred Rogers: America's Favorite Neighbor (television documentary), 2003.

text: Our world hangs like a magnificent jewel in the vastness of space. Every one of us is a part of that jewel. A facet of that jewel. And in the perspective of infinity, our differences are infinitesimal.
author: Fred Rogers
citation: Commencement Address at Dartmouth College June 9th, 2002

text: It’s not the honors and the prizes and the fancy outsides of life which ultimately nourish our souls. It’s the knowing that we can be trusted, that we never have to fear the truth, that the bedrock of our very being is good stuff.
author: Fred Rogers
citation: Commencement Address at Middlebury College May, 2001

text: It’s our insides that make us who we are, that allow us to dream and wonder and feel for others. That’s what’s essential. That’s what will always make the biggest difference in our world.
author: Fred Rogers
citation: Commencement Address at Middlebury College May, 2001

text: If only you could sense how important you are to the lives of those you meet; how important you can be to people you may never even dream of. There is something of yourself that you leave at every meeting with another person.
author: Fred Rogers
citation: Mister Rogers' Neighborhood: Thoughts For All Ages

text: As a writer, one has to be willing to be wrong, willing to make mistakes. I’ve put everything on the table and accepted the fact that I may come up short. And, if (or when) I do, that’s okay.
author: Nikki Giovanni
citation: “Nikki Giovanni: Interview" (2008) · NOTE: On accepting fault as a writer.

text: We must keep moving. If you can’t fly, run; if you can’t run, walk; if you can’t walk, crawl; but by all means keep moving.
author: Martin Luther King Jr.
citation: 1960s · Keep Moving from this Mountain (1960)

text: Dark yesterday can be transformed into bright tomorrow.
author: Martin Luther King Jr.
citation: 1960s · Discerning the Signs of History (1964)

text: Here and there an individual or group dares to love, and rises to the majestic heights of moral maturity. So in a real sense this is a great time to be alive.
author: Martin Luther King Jr.
citation: 1960s · The Quest for Peace and Justice (1964)

text:
For nothing worthy proving can be proven,
Nor yet disproven: wherefore thou be wise,
Cleave ever to the sunnier side of doubt,
And cling to Faith beyond the forms of Faith!
author: Alfred Tennyson
citation: From The Ancient Sage (1885), lines 66-69

text: The shell must break before the bird can fly.
author: Alfred Tennyson
citation: From The Ancient Sage (1885), line 154

text:
Be patient. Our Playwright may show
In some fifth act what this wild Drama means.
author: Alfred Tennyson
citation: The Play, reported in Bartlett's Familiar Quotations, 10th ed. (1919)

text: There is no joy but calm!
author: Alfred Tennyson
citation: The Lotos-Eaters (1832) · Choric Song, st. 2

text: Love will conquer at the last.
author: Alfred Tennyson
citation: Locksley Hall Sixty Years After (1886) · Line 280

text: Strike up a song, my friends, and then to bed.
author: Alfred Tennyson
work: The Foresters, Robin Hood and Maid Marion
citation: The Foresters, Robin Hood and Maid Marion (1892) · Act I, Scene III

text: I still need more healthy rest in order to work at my best. My health is the main capital I have and I want to administer it intelligently.
author: Ernest Hemingway
citation: Letter (21 February 1952); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

text: We are all apprentices in a craft where no one ever becomes a master.
author: Ernest Hemingway
citation: New York Journal-American (11 July 1961)

text: I learned never to empty the well of my writing, but always to stop when there was still something there in the deep part of the well, and let it refill at night from the springs that fed it.
author: Ernest Hemingway
citation: As quoted in Reporting (1964) by Lillian Ross

text: Now is no time to think of what you do not have. Think of what you can do with what there is.
author: Ernest Hemingway
work: The Old Man and the Sea
citation: The Old Man and the Sea (1952)

text: I would stand and look out over the roofs of Paris and think, “Do not worry. You have always written before and you will write now. All you have to do is write one true sentence. Write the truest sentence you know.”
author: Ernest Hemingway
citation: A Moveable Feast (1964) · Ch. 2

text: Fortunately I have never learned to take the good advice I give myself nor the counsel of my fears.
author: Ernest Hemingway
citation: The Dangerous Summer (1985) · Ch. 1

text: Where we find a difficulty we may always expect that a discovery awaits us. Where there is cover we hope for game.
author: C. S. Lewis
citation: Reflections on the Psalms (1958), ch. III: Cursings

text: Gratitude looks to the past and love to the present; fear, avarice, lust, and ambition look ahead.
author: C. S. Lewis
citation: The Screwtape Letters (1942) · Letter XVI

text: We live, in fact, in a world starved for solitude, silence, and privacy: and therefore starved for meditation and true friendship.
author: C. S. Lewis
work: The Weight of Glory and Other Addresses
citation: The Weight of Glory and Other Addresses (1949) · "Membership"

text: But how can the characters in a play guess the plot? We are not the playwright, we are not the producer, we are not even the audience. We are on the stage. To play well the scenes in which we are “on” concerns us much more than to guess about the scenes that follow it.
author: C. S. Lewis
citation: The World's Last Night (1952)

text: Eating and reading are two pleasures that combine admirably.
author: C. S. Lewis
citation: Surprised by Joy (1955) · Ch. IX: "The Great Knock"

text: We are born helpless. As soon as we are fully conscious we discover loneliness. We need others physically, emotionally, intellectually; we need them if we are to know anything, even ourselves.
author: C. S. Lewis
citation: The Four Loves (1960) · Introduction

text: Friendship is unnecessary, like philosophy, like art, like the universe itself (for God did not need to create). It has no survival value; rather it is one of those things which give value to survival.
author: C. S. Lewis
citation: The Four Loves (1960) · Ch. IV

text: Enough work to do, and strength enough to do the work.
author: Rudyard Kipling
citation: Other works · A Doctor's Work, an address at Middlesex Hospital (October 1908).

text: More men are killed by overwork than the importance of the world justifies.
author: Rudyard Kipling
citation: Other works · The Phantom 'Rickshaw (1888).

text:
Ever the wide world over, lass,
Ever the trail held true,
Over the world and under the world,
And back at the last to you.
author: Rudyard Kipling
citation: Other works · The Gypsy Trail, Stanza 2 (1892).

text: Seize the moments of happiness, love and be loved! That is the only reality in the world, all else is folly. It is the one thing we are interested in here.
author: Leo Tolstoy
citation: War and Peace (1865–1867; 1869) · Book IV, Ch. 11

text: The strongest of all warriors are these two — Time and Patience.
author: Leo Tolstoy
citation: War and Peace (1865–1867; 1869) · Bk. X, ch. 16

text: Pure and complete sorrow is as impossible as pure and complete joy.
author: Leo Tolstoy
citation: War and Peace (1865–1867; 1869) · Bk. XV, ch. 1

text: The primary indication, to my thinking, of a well-ordered mind is a man’s ability to remain in one place and linger in his own company.
author: Seneca
citation: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) · Letter II: On discursiveness in reading

text: “What progress, you ask, have I made? I have begun to be a friend to myself.” That was indeed a great benefit; such a person can never be alone. You may be sure that such a man is a friend to all mankind.
author: Seneca
citation: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) · Letter VI: On precepts and exemplars · Seneca is quoting Hecato.

text: It is indeed foolish to be unhappy now because you may be unhappy at some future time.
author: Seneca
citation: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) · Letter XXIV: On despising death

text: You must lay aside the burdens of the mind; until you do this, no place will satisfy you.
author: Seneca
citation: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) · Letter XXVIII: On travel as a cure for discontent

text: I am endeavouring to live every day as if it were a complete life.
author: Seneca
citation: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) · Letter LXI: On meeting death cheerfully

text: Two elements must therefore be rooted out once for all—the fear of future suffering, and the recollection of past suffering; since the latter no longer concerns me, and the former concerns me not yet.
author: Seneca
citation: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) · Letter LXXVIII: On the Healing Power of the Mind

text: Accept in an unruffled spirit that which is inevitable.
author: Seneca
citation: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) · Letter XCIX: On Consolation to the Bereaved

text: Therefore, my dear Lucilius, begin at once to live, and count each separate day as a separate life.
author: Seneca
citation: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) · Letter CI: On the Futility of Planning Ahead

text: Apply reason to difficulties; harsh circumstances can be softened, narrow limits can be widened, and burdensome things can be made to press less severely on those who bear them cleverly.
author: Seneca
citation: On Tranquility of the Mind

text: The mind must be indulged, and leisure must be given from time to time, which is the place of food and strength.
author: Seneca
citation: Dialogues · Dialogi de Tranquillitate Animi (Concerning Peace of Mind)

text: I do not ask you about the dead past. I bring you to the living present.
author: Frederick Douglass
citation: 1860s · Should the Negro Enlist in the Union Army? (1863)

text: Hope is definitely not the same thing as optimism. It is not the conviction that something will turn out well, but the certainty that something makes sense, regardless of how it turns out.
author: Václav Havel
citation: Disturbing the Peace (1986) · Ch. 5 : The Politics of Hope

text:
Elected Silence, sing to me
And beat upon my whorlèd ear,
Pipe me to pastures still and be
The music that I care to hear.
author: Gerard Manley Hopkins
citation: Wessex Poems and Other Verses (1918) · "The Habit of Perfection", lines 1-4

text:
The world is charged with the grandeur of God.
It will flame out, like shining from shook foil;
It gathers to a greatness, like the ooze of oil
Crushed.
author: Gerard Manley Hopkins
citation: Wessex Poems and Other Verses (1918) · "God's Grandeur", lines 1-4

text: There lives the dearest freshness deep down things.
author: Gerard Manley Hopkins
citation: Wessex Poems and Other Verses (1918) · "God's Grandeur," line 10

text:
Look at the stars! look, look up at the skies!
O look at all the fire-folk sitting in the air!
The bright boroughs, the circle-citadels there!
author: Gerard Manley Hopkins
citation: Wessex Poems and Other Verses (1918) · "The Starlight Night" (1877), lines 1-3

author: Gerard Manley Hopkins
citation: Wessex Poems and Other Verses (1918) · "Pied Beauty", lines 1-3

text:
Ask of her, the mighty mother:
Her reply puts this other
Question: What is Spring?—
Growth in everything.
author: Gerard Manley Hopkins
citation: Wessex Poems and Other Verses (1918) · "The May Magnificat", stanza 4

text:
What would the world be, once bereft
Of wet and of wildness? Let them be left,
O let them be left, wildness and wet;
Long live the weeds and the wilderness yet.
author: Gerard Manley Hopkins
citation: Wessex Poems and Other Verses (1918) · "Inversnaid, lines 13-16

text:
I say that we are wound
With mercy round and round
As if with air.
author: Gerard Manley Hopkins
citation: Wessex Poems and Other Verses (1918) · "The Blessed Virgin compared to the Air we Breathe", lines 34-36

text:
My own heart let me have more have pity on; let
Me live to my sad self hereafter kind,
Charitable; not live this tormented mind
With this tormented mind tormenting yet.
author: Gerard Manley Hopkins
citation: Wessex Poems and Other Verses (1918) · "My own heart let me have more have pity on", lines 1-4

text: Mine, O thou lord of life, send my roots rain.
author: Gerard Manley Hopkins
citation: Wessex Poems and Other Verses (1918) · "Thou art indeed just, Lord, if I contend", line 14

text: When one door of happiness closes, another opens; but often we look so long at the closed door that we do not see the one which has been opened for us.
author: Helen Keller
citation: We Bereaved (1929)

text: Believe, when you are most unhappy, that there is something for you to do in the world. So long as you can sweeten another’s pain, life is not in vain.
author: Helen Keller
citation: We Bereaved (1929)

text: Security is mostly a superstition. It does not exist in nature, nor do the children of men as a whole experience it. Avoiding danger is no safer in the long run than outright exposure. Life is either a daring adventure, or nothing.
author: Helen Keller
citation: The Open Door (1957) This quotation is often contracted into: Security is mostly a superstition... Life is either a daring adventure, or nothing. or paraphrased: Life is either a daring adventure or nothing at all.

text: I would rather walk with a friend in the dark than walk alone in the light.
author: Helen Keller
citation: "Helen and Teacher: The Story of Helen Keller and Anne Sullivan Macy", Joseph P. Lash (1980)

text: It seemed to me that there could be nothing more beautiful than the sun, whose warmth makes all things grow.
author: Helen Keller
citation: The Story of My Life (1903) · Ch. 6

text: The beautiful truth burst upon my mind — I felt that there were invisible lines stretched between my spirit and the spirits of others.
author: Helen Keller
citation: The Story of My Life (1903) · Ch. 6

text: I trust, and nothing that happens disturbs my trust.
author: Helen Keller
citation: Optimism (1903)

text: Optimism, then, is a fact within my own heart. But as I look out upon life, my heart meets no contradiction. The outward world justifies my inward universe of good.
author: Helen Keller
citation: Optimism (1903)

text: Optimism is the faith that leads to achievement; nothing can be done without hope.
author: Helen Keller
citation: Optimism (1903)

text: So long as the memory of certain beloved friends lives in my heart I shall say that life is good.
author: Helen Keller
citation: Midstream (1929)

text: I who cannot see find hundreds of things to interest me through mere touch.
author: Helen Keller
citation: Three Days to See (1933)

text: I feel the delightful, velvety texture of a flower, and discover its remarkable convolutions; and something of the miracle of Nature is revealed to me.
author: Helen Keller
citation: Three Days to See (1933)

text: A happy life consists not in the absence, but in the mastery of hardships.
author: Helen Keller
citation: The Simplest Way to be Happy (1933)

text:
Whatever’s lost, it first was won;
We will not struggle nor impugn.
Perhaps the cup was broken here,
That Heaven’s new wine might show more clear.
I praise Thee while my days go on.
author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
citation: Last Poems (1862) · "De Profundis", st. 22

text: We may be surprised at the people we find in heaven. God has a soft spot for sinners. His standards are quite low.
author: Desmond Tutu
citation: As quoted in The Mammoth Book of Zingers, Quips, and One-Liners (2004) by Geoff Tibballs, p. 255

text: All are to be held in the incredible embrace of the love that won’t let us go.
author: Desmond Tutu
citation: "And God Smiles," sermon preached at All Saints Church, Pasadena, California (6 November 2005)

text: Sometimes you want to whisper in God’s ear, “God, we know you are in charge, but why don’t you make it slightly more obvious?”
author: Desmond Tutu
citation: Wallenberg Lecture (2008)

text: If you are wholly perplexed and in straits, have patience, for patience is the key to joy.
author: Rumi
citation: Masnavi · I, 2908 (tr. Helminski, 1990)

text: God turns you from one feeling to another and teaches by means of opposites, so that you will have two wings to fly, not one.
author: Rumi
citation: Masnavi · II, 1552; 1554 (tr. Helminski, 1990)

text:
That which God said to the rose,
and caused it to laugh in full-blown beauty,
He said to my heart,
and made it a hundred times more beautiful.
author: Rumi
citation: Masnavi · III, 4129 (tr. Helminski, 1996)

author: Rumi
citation: Divan-i Shams · 1740:1-3 (tr. Fatemeh Keshavarz, 1998)

text: I loafe and invite my soul.
author: Walt Whitman
citation: Bartlett's Familiar Quotations, 10th ed. (1919) · Song of Myself, 1

text:
Each of us inevitable;
Each of us limitless—each of us with his or her right upon the earth.
author: Walt Whitman
citation: Bartlett's Familiar Quotations, 10th ed. (1919) · Salut au Monde, 11

text: Give me the splendid silent sun, with all his beams full-dazzling!
author: Walt Whitman
work: Drum-Taps. Give me the splendid Silent Sun
citation: Bartlett's Familiar Quotations, 10th ed. (1919) · Drum-Taps. Give me the splendid Silent Sun

text:
To me every hour of the light and dark is a miracle,
Every cubic inch of space is a miracle.
author: Walt Whitman
citation: Bartlett's Familiar Quotations, 10th ed. (1919) · Miracles

text:
The paths to the house I seek to make,
But leave to those to come the house itself.
author: Walt Whitman
work: Thou Mother with thy Equal Brood
citation: Bartlett's Familiar Quotations, 10th ed. (1919) · Thou Mother with thy Equal Brood, 1

text: Surely something resides in this heart that is not perishable, and life is more than a dream.
author: Mary Wollstonecraft
citation: Letters Written in Sweden (1796)

text: Believe in life! Always human beings will progress to greater, broader, and fuller life.
author: W. E. B. Du Bois
citation: Last message to the world (written 1957); read at his funeral (1963)

text: Dear sisters and brothers, we realise the importance of light when we see darkness. We realise the importance of our voice when we are silenced.
author: Malala Yousafzai
citation: UN speech, June 2013

text: Every individual matters. Every individual has a role to play. Every individual makes a difference.
author: Jane Goodall
citation: 1990s · With Love (1999)

text: All my life through, the new sights of Nature made me rejoice like a child.
author: Marie Curie
citation: Pierre Curie (1923), as translated by Charlotte Kellogg and Vernon Lyman Kellogg, p. 162

text: I was taught that the way of progress was neither swift nor easy.
author: Marie Curie
citation: Java Connector Architecture: Building Custom Connectors and Adapters‎ (2002) by Atul Apte, p. 69

text: In life, there’s nothing to be feared, everything is to be understood.
author: Marie Curie
citation: As quoted in Our Precarious Habitat (2006) by Melvin A. Benarde

text: Where there’s hope, there’s life. It fills us with fresh courage and makes us strong again.
author: Anne Frank
work: The Diary of a Young Girl
citation: The Diary of a Young Girl (1942 - 1944) · 1944 · Date?

text: The good life is a process, not a state of being. It is a direction not a destination.
author: Carl Rogers
citation: Person to person: The problem of being human: A new trend in psychology (1967) · Source: page 187.

text: I urge you to please notice when you are happy, and exclaim or murmur or think at some point, “If this isn’t nice, I don’t know what is.”
author: Kurt Vonnegut
citation: Various quotations · "Knowing What's Nice", an essay from In These Times (2003)

text: And a step backward, after making a wrong turn, is a step in the right direction.
author: Kurt Vonnegut
citation: Player Piano (1952) · Chapter 32 (p. 295)

text: His poor soul was flooded with pleasure as he realized that one friend was all that a man needed in order to be well-supplied with friendship.
author: Kurt Vonnegut
citation: The Sirens of Titan (1959) · Chapter 11 "We Hate Malachi Constant Because..." (p. 259)

text: Everything was beautiful and nothing hurt.
author: Kurt Vonnegut
citation: Slaughterhouse-Five (1969)

text: You are pooped and demoralized. Why wouldn’t you be? Of course it is exhausting, having to reason all the time in a universe which wasn’t meant to be reasonable.
author: Kurt Vonnegut
citation: Breakfast of Champions (1973)

text: Many people need desperately to receive this message: “I feel and think much as you do, care about many of the things you care about, although most people don’t care about them. You are not alone.”
author: Kurt Vonnegut
citation: Timequake (1997)

text: We are here on Earth to fart around. Don’t let anybody tell you any different.
author: Kurt Vonnegut
citation: A Man Without a Country (2005)

text: The arts are not a way to make a living. They are a very human way of making life more bearable. Practicing an art, no matter how well or badly, is a way to make your soul grow, for heaven’s sake.
author: Kurt Vonnegut
citation: A Man Without a Country (2005)

text: We have to continually be jumping off cliffs and developing our wings on the way down.
author: Kurt Vonnegut
citation: If This Isn't Nice, What Is?: Advice for the Young (2013)

text:
Pleasures newly found are sweet
When they lie about our feet.
author: William Wordsworth
citation: To the Small Celandine ("Pleasures Newly Found are Sweet"), st. 1 (wr. 1803; pub. 1807)

text:
Every gift of noble origin
Is breathed upon by Hope’s perpetual breath.
author: William Wordsworth
citation: These Times, l. 10 (wr. 1803; pub. 1815)

text:
Dreams, books, are each a world; and books, we know,
Are a substantial world, both pure and good:
Round these, with tendrils strong as flesh and blood,
Our pastime and our happiness will grow.
author: William Wordsworth
citation: Personal Talk. Sonnets, no. 3 (wr. 1806; pub. 1807)

text:
It is a beauteous evening, calm and free,
The holy time is quiet as a Nun
Breathless with adoration; the broad sun
Is sinking down in its tranquillity;
The gentleness of heaven broods o’er the Sea.
author: William Wordsworth
citation: It Is a Beautious Evening, l. 1 (wr. 1802; pub. 1807)

text: Surprised by joy—impatient as the Wind.
author: William Wordsworth
citation: Surprised by Joy, l. 1 (1815)

text:
Through love, through hope, and faith’s transcendent dower,
We feel that we are greater than we know.
author: William Wordsworth
citation: The River Duddon, sonnet 34 - Afterthought, l. 13 (1820)

text:
Small service is true service while it lasts.
Of humblest friends, bright creature! scorn not one:
The daisy, by the shadow that it casts,
Protects the lingering dewdrop from the sun.
author: William Wordsworth
work: To a Child. Written in her Album
citation: To a Child. Written in her Album (1834)

text:
Come forth into the light of things,
Let Nature be your teacher.
author: William Wordsworth
citation: Lyrical Ballads (1798; 1800; 1802) · The Tables Turned, st. 4 (1798)

text:
One impulse from a vernal wood
May teach you more of man,
Of moral evil and of good,
Than all the sages can.
author: William Wordsworth
citation: Lyrical Ballads (1798; 1800; 1802) · The Tables Turned, st. 6 (1798)

text:
I wandered lonely as a cloud
That floats on high o’er vales and hills,
When all at once I saw a crowd,
A host, of golden daffodils.
Beside the lake, beneath the trees,
Fluttering and dancing in the breeze.
author: William Wordsworth
work: I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud
citation: I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud (1804) · Stanza 1

text:
That inward eye
Which is the bliss of solitude.
author: William Wordsworth
work: I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud
citation: I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud (1804) · Stanza 4

text:
For the gods approve
The depth, and not the tumult, of the soul.
author: William Wordsworth
citation: Laodamia (1814) · Stanza 13

text:
And ‘t is my faith, that every flower
Enjoys the air it breathes.
author: William Wordsworth
citation: Bartlett's Familiar Quotations, 10th ed. (1919) · Lines written in Early Spring

text:
Up! up! my friend, and quit your books,
Or surely you ‘ll grow double!
Up! up! my friend, and clear your looks!
Why all this toil and trouble?
author: William Wordsworth
citation: Bartlett's Familiar Quotations, 10th ed. (1919) · The Tables Turned

text: One of those heavenly days that cannot die.
author: William Wordsworth
citation: Bartlett's Familiar Quotations, 10th ed. (1919) · Nutting

text: It’s even pleasant to be sick when you know that there are people who await your recovery as they might await a holiday.
author: Anton Chekhov
work: The Story of an Unknown Man
citation: The Story of an Unknown Man or An Anonymous Story, ch. 15 (1893)

text: It is unfortunate that we try to solve the simplest questions cleverly, and therefore make them unusually complicated. We should seek a simple solution.
author: Anton Chekhov
citation: Note-Book of Anton Chekhov (1921)

text: There is no Monday which will not give its place to Tuesday.
author: Anton Chekhov
citation: Note-Book of Anton Chekhov (1921)

text: The wealthy man is not he who has money, but he who has the means to live in the luxurious state of early spring.
author: Anton Chekhov
citation: Letters · Letter to L.A. Avilova (April 29, 1892)

text: What seems to us serious, significant and important will, in future times, be forgotten or won’t seem important at all.
author: Anton Chekhov
citation: The Three Sisters (1901) · Act I

text: It is a time of quiet joy, the sunny morning. When the glittery dew is on the mallow weeds, each leaf holds a jewel which is beautiful if not valuable. This is no time for hurry or for bustle. Thoughts are slow and deep and golden in the morning.
author: John Steinbeck
citation: Tortilla Flat (1935) · Ch. 4

text: Sometimes a kind of glory lights up the mind of a man. It happens to nearly everyone.
author: John Steinbeck
citation: East of Eden (1952) · Part 2, Ch. 13. i

text: Men do change, and change comes like a little wind that ruffles the curtains at dawn, and it comes like the stealthy perfume of wildflowers hidden in the grass.

And earthly change from pain to pain,

Danger, and guilt, and darkness lie,

We hold a bright, untroubled sky,
Warm with ten thousand mingled rays
Of suns that know no winter days?

And this soul forget its sorrow
And the rose ray of the closing day
May promise a brighter morrow.

Shook down on me
The dust of snow

A change of mood

author: Robert Frost

Dig And Be Dug
