text: The greatest mistake you can make in life is to be continually fearing you will make one.
author: Elbert Hubbard
work: The Note Book of Elbert Hubbard (1927)
citation: Elbert Hubbard, The Note Book of Elbert Hubbard (1927)

text: Fear? What has a man to do with fear? Chance rules our lives, and the future is all unknown. Best live as we may, from day to day.
author: Sophocles
citation: Sophocles, Jocasta (Line 977?) in Oedipus Rex

text: Nature, even when she is scant and thin outwardly, satisfies us still by the assurance of a certain generosity at the roots.
author: Henry David Thoreau
work: A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers
citation: Henry David Thoreau, A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers (1849).

text: In God’s world, for those who are in earnest there is no failure. No work truly done, no word earnestly spoken, no sacrifice freely made, was ever made in vain.
author: Frederick William Robertson
citation: Frederick William Robertson, quoted in Daily Strength for Daily Needs, compiled by Mary Wilder Tileston (entry for April 5).

text: All that we have to decide is what to do with the time that is given us.
author: J. R. R. Tolkien
citation: J. R. R. Tolkien, said by Gandalf in The Fellowship of the Rings

text: The Great Western Disease is that we fixate on the future at the expense of enjoying the life we’re living now.
author: Marshall Goldsmith
work: What Got You Here Won’t Get You There
citation: Marshall Goldsmith (2010), What Got You Here Won't Get You There. p. 81

text: I do not want to foresee the future. I am concerned with taking care of the present. God has given me no control over the moment following.
author: Mahatma Gandhi
citation: Mahatma Gandhi, in Anthony Parel Gandhi, Freedom, and Self-rule, Lexington Books, 1 January 2000, p. 59

text: The wisely cultivated man, conscious how insignificant a drop he is in the vast stream of life, learns his limitation, and accepts events with modesty and equanimity.
author: Henry Maudsley
work: Dictionary of Burning Words of Brilliant Writers
citation: Henry Maudsley, Dictionary of Burning Words of Brilliant Writers (1895) p. 333.

text: I see that time divided is never long, and that regularity abridges all things.
author: Abel Stevens
citation: Abel Stevens, Life of Madame de Staël, Chapter XXXVIII

text: Time ripens all things. No man is born wise.
author: Miguel de Cervantes
citation: Miguel de Cervantes, Don Quixote de la Mancha (1605–1615), chapter 33. Note: "Time ripens all things" is the translator's interpolation and does not appear in the original Spanish text.

text:
Yes! in the poor man’s garden grow,
Far more than herbs and flowers,
Kind thoughts, contentment, peace of mind,
And joy for weary hours.
author: Mary Howitt
citation: Mary Howitt, The Poor Man's Garden.

text: Though patience be a tired mare, yet she will plod.
author: William Shakespeare
citation: William Shakespeare, Henry V Act II, scene i.

text:
And Rest, that strengthens unto virtuous deeds,
Is one with Prayer.
author: Bayard Taylor
citation: Bayard Taylor, "The Temptation of Hassan Ben Khaled", Stanza 4, in Poems of the Orient (Boston: Ticknor and Fields, 1855), p. 25.

text: Nature is painting for us, day after day, pictures of infinite beauty.
author: John Ruskin
citation: John Ruskin, (1819-1900).

text: As you cannot have a sweet and wholesome abode unless you admit the air and sunshine freely into your rooms, so a strong body and a bright, happy, or serene countenance can only result from the free admittance into the mind of thoughts of joy and good will and serenity.
author: James Allen
citation: James Allen, in As A Man Thinketh (1902), Ch. 3 : Effect of Thought on Health and the Body

text: Nothing can bring you peace but yourself. Nothing can bring you peace but the triumph of principles.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: Ralph Waldo Emerson, "Of Self-Reliance", Essays, First Series (1841)

text:
How calm, how beautiful comes on
The stilly hour, when storms are gone!
When warring winds have died away,
And clouds, beneath the glancing ray,
Melt off, and leave the land and sea
Sleeping in bright tranquillity!
author: Thomas Moore
citation: Thomas Moore, Lalla Rookh (1817), Fire Worshippers, Stanza 62.

text:
O magic sleep! O comfortable bird,
That broodest o’er the troubled sea of the mind
Till it is hush’d and smooth! O unconfined
Restraint! imprisoned liberty! great key
To golden palaces.
author: John Keats
citation: John Keats, Endymion (1818), Book I, line 452.

text: If you want to go faster, then don’t walk, do something else: drive, slide or fly. Don’t walk. And when you are walking, there is only one sort of performance that counts: the brilliance of the sky, the splendour of the landscape. Walking is not a sport.
author: Frédéric Gros
citation: Frédéric Gros, in A Philosophy of Walking (2008), Ch. 1: Walking Is Not a Sport; as translated by John Howe (2014)

text: Nothing is so much to be feared as fear.
author: Henry David Thoreau
citation: Henry David Thoreau, Journal (September 7, 1851).

text: However we may receive blows, and however knocked about we may be, the Soul is there and is never injured. We are that Infinite.
author: Swami Vivekananda
citation: Pearls of Wisdom

text:
Happy the man, and happy he alone,
He who can call today his own;
He who, secure within, can say,
Tomorrow, do thy worst, for I have lived today.
author: John Dryden
citation: John Dryden, Imitation of Horace (1685), Book III, Ode 29 line 65-68

text:
‘Tis Noon;—a calm, unbroken sleep
Is on the blue waves of the deep;
A soft haze, like a fairy dream,
Is floating over wood and stream;
And many a broad magnolia flower,
Within its shadowy woodland bower,
Is gleaming like a lovely star.
author: George D. Prentice
citation: George D. Prentice, To an Absent Wife, Stanza 2; published in The Guardian: Volume 4 (1853), p. 115.

text: A master in the art of living draws no sharp distinction between his work and his play; his labor and his leisure; his mind and his body; his education and his recreation. He hardly knows which is which.
author: L. P. Jacks
citation: L. P. Jacks, Education through Recreation (1932), p. 1.

text:
Sweet is the pleasure itself cannot spoil.
Is not true leisure one with true toil?
author: John Sullivan Dwight
citation: John Sullivan Dwight, True Rest.

text:
This is the charm, by sages often told,
Converting all it touches into gold:
Content can soothe, where’er by fortune placed,
Can rear a garden in the desert waste.
author: Henry Kirk White
citation: Henry Kirk White, Clifton Grove, line 130.

text: Patience and shuffle the cards.
author: Miguel de Cervantes
citation: Miguel de Cervantes, Don Quixote (1605-15), Part II, Book I, Chapter VI.

text:
Present fears
Are less than horrible imaginings.
author: William Shakespeare
citation: William Shakespeare, Macbeth (1605), Act I, scene 3, line 137.

text:
I argue not
Against Heaven’s hand or will, nor bate a jot
Of heart or hope; but still bear up and steer
Right onward.
author: John Milton
citation: John Milton, Sonnet, To Cyriack Skinner.

text: Just remember, you can do anything you set your mind to, but it takes action, perseverance, and facing your fears.
author: Gillian Anderson
work: Girl Boss: Running the Show Like the Big Chicks
citation: Gillian Anderson, excerpt from the foreword in Girl Boss: Running the Show Like the Big Chicks (1999)

text:
Life is mostly froth and bubble,
Two things stand like stone,
Kindness in another’s trouble,
Courage in your own.
author: Adam Lindsay Gordon
citation: Adam Lindsay Gordon, "Ye Wearie Wayfarer His Ballad", Fytte VIII: Finis Exoptatus, 15th stanza, in Sea Spray and Smoke Drift (Melbourne: George Robinson, 1867), p. 54.

text: The phrase “work-life balance” tells us that people think that work is the opposite of life. We should be talking about life-life balance.
author: Patrick Dixon
citation: Patrick Dixon, Building a Better Business (2005) p. 182.

text: Our patience will achieve more than our force.
author: Edmund Burke
work: Reflections on the Revolution in France
citation: Edmund Burke Reflections on the Revolution in France.

text: The direst foe of courage is the fear itself, not the object of it; and the man who can overcome his own terror is a hero and more.
author: George MacDonald
citation: George MacDonald, Sir Gibbie, Chapter XX.

text:
Dear little head, that lies in calm content
Within the gracious hollow that God made
In every human shoulder, where He meant
Some tired head for comfort should be laid.
author: Celia Thaxter
citation: Celia Thaxter, Song.

text: Nothing we do can change the past, but everything we do changes the future.
author: Ashleigh Brilliant
citation: Ashleigh Brilliant. As quoted at goodreads.com. Archived from the original on January 9, 2024.

text:
Many strokes, though with a little axe,
Hew down and fell the hardest-timber’d oak.
author: William Shakespeare
citation: William Shakespeare, Henry VI, Part III (c. 1591), Act II, scene 1, line 54.

text: It is a happy talent to know how to play.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: Ralph Waldo Emerson, in Emerson in His Journals, Harvard University Press, 1 January 1984, p. 138

text:
Time for work,—yet take
Much holiday for arts and friendships sake.
author: George James de Wilde
citation: George James de Wilde, Sonnet, On the Arrival of Spring.

text: The use of travelling is to regulate imagination by reality, and instead of thinking how things may be, to see them as they are.
author: Samuel Johnson
citation: Johnsoniana · Piozzi, 102

text: The silence that is in the starry sky.
author: William Wordsworth
work: Song at the Feast of Brougham Castle
citation: William Wordsworth, Song at the Feast of Brougham Castle.

text:
Weep not that the world changes—did it keep
A stable, changeless state, it were cause indeed to weep.
author: William Cullen Bryant
citation: William Cullen Bryant, Mutation. in Hoyt's New Cyclopedia Of Practical Quotations (1922), p. 93-96

text: Every failure is a step to success.
author: William Whewell
citation: William Whewell, Lectures on the History of Moral Philosophy in England, Lecture 7 (1852).

text: Men are in error when they lament the flight of time, accusing it of being too swift, and not perceiving that it is sufficient as it passes; but good memory, with which nature has endowed us, causes things long past to seem present.
author: Leonardo da Vinci
work: The Notebooks of Leonardo Da Vinci
citation: Leonardo da Vinci, The Notebooks of Leonardo Da Vinci (1938), XIX Philosophical Maxims. Morals. Polemics and Speculations., as translated by Edward MacCurdy

text:
Imagination frames events unknown,
In wild, fantastic shapes of hideous ruin,
And what it fears creates.
author: Hannah More
citation: Hannah More, Belshazzar, Part II.

text:
The timely dew of sleep
Now falling with soft slumb’rous weight inclines
Our eyelids.
author: John Milton
citation: John Milton, Paradise Lost (1667; 1674), Book IV, line 615.

text:
And to tired limbs and over-busy thoughts,
Inviting sleep and soft forgetfulness.
author: William Wordsworth
citation: William Wordsworth, The Excursion (1814), Book IV.

text:
Sister Simplicitie!
Sing, sing a song to me,—
Sing me to sleep!
Some legend low and long,
Slow as the summer song
Of the dull Deep.
author: Sidney Dobell
citation: Sidney Dobell, A Sleep Song.

text:
How far your eyes may pierce, I cannot tell;
Striving to better, oft we mar what’s well.
author: William Shakespeare
citation: William Shakespeare, King Lear (1608), Act I, scene 4, line 368.

text:
The brave man is not he who feels no fear,
For that were stupid and irrational;
But he, whose noble soul its fear subdues,
And bravely dares the danger nature shrinks from.
author: Joanna Baillie
citation: Joanna Baillie, Count Basil (1798), Act III, scene 1, line 151.

text: Whatever you accept completely will take you to peace, including the acceptance that you cannot accept, that you are in resistance.
author: Eckhart Tolle
citation: Stillness Speaks (2003) · Ch 6

text: It is not necessary for all men to be great in action. The greatest and sublimest power is often simple patience.
author: Horace Bushnell
work: Dictionary of Burning Words of Brilliant Writers
citation: Horace Bushnell, p. 443.

text:
He tires betimes that spurs too fast betimes;
With eager feeding food doth choke the feeder.
author: William Shakespeare
citation: William Shakespeare, Richard II (c. 1595), Act II, scene 1, line 36.

text: True contentment depends not upon what we have; a tub was large enough for Diogenes, but a world was too little for Alexander.
author: Charles Caleb Colton
work: Dictionary of Burning Words of Brilliant Writers
citation: Charles Caleb Colton, p. 161.

text: Rest is not idleness, and to lie sometimes on the grass under the trees on a summer’s day, listening to the murmur of water, or watching the clouds float across the blue sky, is by no means waste of time.
author: John Lubbock
citation: John Lubbock, The Use of Life (1894)

text: A life spent in making mistakes is not only more honorable but more useful than a life spent doing nothing.
author: George Bernard Shaw
work: The Doctor’s Dilemma: Preface on Doctors
citation: George Bernard Shaw, The Doctor's Dilemma: Preface on Doctors (1909)

text: Whereas before you dwelt in time and paid brief visits to the Now, have your dwelling place in the Now and pay brief visits to past and future when required to deal with the practical aspects of your life situation.
author: Eckhart Tolle
citation: Eckhart Tolle, The Power of Now.

author: William Shakespeare
citation: William Shakespeare, Julius Cæsar (1599), Act II, scene 1, line 229.

text: A great change in life is like a cold bath in winter — we all hesitate at the first plunge.
author: Letitia Elizabeth Landon
citation: Letitia Elizabeth Landon, Romance and Reality (1831), Vol. I, Chapter 3

text: Acceptance. Acceptance of the impermanence of being. And acceptance of the imperfect nature of being, or possibly the perfect nature of being, depending on how one looks at it. Acceptance that this is not a rehearsal. That this is it.
author: William Gibson
citation: William Gibson, when asked what will save humanity, in No Maps for These Territories (2000).

text: A man ought to read just as inclination leads him; for what he reads as a task will do him little good.
author: Samuel Johnson
citation: Life of Samuel Johnson (1791) · Vol I · (14 July 1763) p. 121

text: Those who make no mistakes are making the biggest mistakes of all — they are attempting nothing new.
author: Anthony de Mello
citation: Anthony de Mello, One Minute Nonsense (1992), p. 20.

text:
Measure not the work
Until the day’s out and the labour done,
Then bring your gauges.
author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
citation: Elizabeth Barrett Browning, Aurora Leigh (1857), Book V.

text: I like work; it fascinates me. I can sit and look at it for hours. I love to keep it by me: the idea of getting rid of it nearly breaks my heart.
author: Jerome K. Jerome
citation: Jerome K. Jerome, Three Men in a Boat, Chapter XV.

text: I never expect to see a perfect work from imperfect man.
author: Alexander Hamilton
citation: Alexander Hamilton, Federalist No. 85 (August 13/16, 1788; in Benjamin F. Wright, ed., The Federalist (1961), p. 544.

text:
Tender handed stroke a nettle,
And it stings you for your pains;
Grasp it like a man of mettle,
And it soft as silks remains.
author: Aaron Hill
citation: Aaron Hill, Verses Written on a Window.

text: Who can wrestle against Sleep?—Yet is that giant very gentleness.
author: Martin Tupper
citation: Martin Tupper, Of Beauty.

text:
A flower more sacred than far-seen success
Perfumes my solitary path; I find
Sweet compensation in my humbleness,
And reap the harvest of a quiet mind.
author: John Townsend Trowbridge
citation: John Townsend Trowbridge, Twoscore and Ten, Stanza 28.

text:
And Nature does require
Her times of preservation, which perforce
I, her frail son, amongst my brethren mortal,
Must give my tendance to.
author: William Shakespeare
citation: William Shakespeare, Henry VIII (c. 1613), Act III, scene 2, line 147.

text:
The mind is its own place, and in itself
Can make a heaven of hell, a hell of heaven.
author: John Milton
citation: John Milton, Paradise Lost (1667; 1674), Book I, line 254.

text: Wisely, and slow; they stumble that run fast.
author: William Shakespeare
citation: William Shakespeare, Romeo and Juliet (1597), Act II, scene 3, line 94.

text: Not much talk—a great, sweet silence.
author: Henry James, Jr.
citation: Henry James, Jr., A Bundle of Letters, Letter IV.

text: The perfection of a clock is not to go fast, but to be accurate.
author: Luc de Clapiers, Marquis de Vauvenargues
citation: Luc de Clapiers, Marquis de Vauvenargues, Reflections and Maxims, E. Lee, trans. (1903), p. 177.

text: In your patience ye are strong.
author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
work: Dictionary of Burning Words of Brilliant Writers
citation: Elizabeth Barrett Browning, p. 444.

text: Time is the nurse and breeder of all good.
author: William Shakespeare
citation: William Shakespeare, The Two Gentlemen of Verona (1590s), Act III, scene 1, line 243

text: Live in the present and shape the future, do not be casting lingering looks to the distant past for the past has passed away, never again to return.
author: Subramanya Bharathi
citation: Subramanya Bharathi, as quoted in "The People's Poet" by N. Nandhivarman in TamilSydney (7 January 2008)

text: Fear is real and there is nothing you can do about it except to keep functioning, keep your hands and legs and body moving, your mind focused on the task at hand.
author: Alvah Bessie
work: Men in Battle: A Story of Americans in Spain
citation: Alvah Bessie, Men in Battle: A Story of Americans in Spain (1939), p. 241

text: Nothing can be done at once hastily and prudently.
author: Syrus
citation: Syrus, Maxims. 357.

text: Silence is the element in which great things fashion themselves together; that at length they may emerge, full-formed and majestic, into the daylight of Life, which they are thenceforth to rule.
author: Thomas Carlyle
citation: Thomas Carlyle, Sartor Resartus (1833–1834), Book III, chapter 3.

text: The first thing necessary for a constructive dealing with time is to learn to live in the reality of the present moment. For psychologically speaking, this present moment is all we have.
author: Rollo May
citation: Rollo May, Man's Search for Himself (1953), p. 227

text: Our language has wisely sensed the two sides of being alone. It has created the word loneliness to express the pain of being alone. And it has created the word solitude to express the glory of being alone.
author: Paul Tillich
citation: Paul Tillich, The Eternal Now (New York: Scribner, 1963), p. 11

text: He that will have a cake out of the wheat must tarry the grinding.
author: William Shakespeare
citation: William Shakespeare, Troilus and Cressida Act I, scene i.

text:
Nor rural sights alone, but rural sounds,
Exhilarate the spirit, and restore
The tone of languid Nature.
author: William Cowper
citation: William Cowper, The Task (1785), Book I. The Sofa, line 187.

text:
The streams with softest sound are flowing,
The grass you almost hear it growing,
You hear it now, if e’er you can.
author: William Wordsworth
citation: William Wordsworth, The Idiot Boy, Stanza 57.

text: If failure has the strength to turn your life into bitterness itself, then patience has the strength to turn your life into the sweetest joy. Do not surrender to fate after a single failure. Failure, at most, precedes success.
author: Sri Chinmoy
citation: Sri Chinmoy, Songs of the Soul (1971).

text:
I would like to offer one short poem you can recite from time to time, while breathing and smiling:
Breathing in, I calm my body.
Breathing out, I smile.
Dwelling in the present moment
I know this is a wonderful moment.
author: Thich Nhat Hanh
citation: Thích Nhất Hạnh in Being Peace (1987)

text: Man only plays when in the full meaning of the word he is a man, and he is only completely a man when he plays.
author: Friedrich Schiller
citation: Friedrich Schiller, The Aesthetic Education of Man, Fifteenth Letter

text: Not living in fear is a great gift, because certainly these days we do it so much. And do you know what I like about comedy? You can’t laugh and be afraid at the same time—of anything. If you’re laughing, I defy you to be afraid.
author: Stephen Colbert
citation: Stephen Colbert Parade interview (23 September 2007)

text: It is in your power to withdraw yourself whenever you desire. Perfect tranquility within consists in the good ordering of the mind, the realm of your own.
author: Marcus Aurelius
work: Treasures of love & inspiration Galahad Books
citation: Marcus Aurelius, in Treasures of love & inspiration Galahad Books, 1993, p. 278

text: Those who aim at faultless regularity will only produce mediocrity, and no one ever approaches perfection except by stealth, and unknown to themselves.
author: William Hazlitt
citation: William Hazlitt, "Thoughts on Taste", The Edinburgh Magazine, July 1819.

text: There are few things more liberating in this life than having your worst fear realized.
author: Conan O'Brien
citation: Conan O'Brien, Commencement Address at Dartmouth College, 2011

text:
And silence, like a poultice, comes
To heal the blows of sound.
author: Oliver Wendell Holmes, Sr.
citation: Oliver Wendell Holmes, Sr., The Music Grinder.

text: With engineering, I view this year’s failure as next year’s opportunity to try it again. Failures are not something to be avoided. You want to have them happen as quickly as you can so you can make progress rapidly.
author: Gordon Moore
citation: Gordon Moore,

text: Just as the moon has no light of its own, but can only reflect the light of the sun, so are past and future only pale reflections of the light, power, and reality of the eternal present. Their reality is “borrowed” from the Now.
author: Eckhart Tolle
citation: Eckhart Tolle, The Power of Now.

text: A man’s labors must pass like the sunrises and sunsets of the world. The next thing, not the last, must be his care.
author: George MacDonald
work: Dictionary of Burning Words of Brilliant Writers
citation: George MacDonald, p. 369.

text:
Or in the night, imagining some fear,
How easy is a bush suppos’d a bear!
author: William Shakespeare
citation: William Shakespeare, A Midsummer Night's Dream (c. 1595-96), Act V, scene 1, line 21.

text: There is no secret to balance. You just have to feel the waves.
author: Frank Herbert
citation: Frank Herbert quoted in “21 Keys to Work/Life Balance: Unlock Your Full Potential” p. 10.

text: Second thoughts oftentimes are the very worst of all thoughts.
author: William Shenstone
work: Detached Thoughts on Men and Manners
citation: William Shenstone, Detached Thoughts on Men and Manners; Reported in Hoyt's New Cyclopedia Of Practical Quotations (1922), p. 787-90

text: To me the greatest moment in an experiment is always just before I learn whether the particular idea is a good or a bad one. Thus even a failure is exciting, and most of my ideas have of course been wrong.
author: Ivar Giaever
citation: Ivar Giaever, Electron Tunneling and Superconductivity, Nobel Lecture (December 12, 1973).

text: The road to wisdom? Well, it’s plain and simple to express: Err, and err, and err again. But less, and less, and less.
author: Piet Hein
citation: Piet Hein, Grooks (1966)

text: Let me assert my firm belief that the only thing we have to fear is fear itself—nameless, unreasoning, unjustified terror which paralyzes needed efforts to convert retreat into advance.
author: Franklin D. Roosevelt
citation: Franklin D. Roosevelt, inaugural address (March 4, 1933); in The Public Papers and Addresses of Franklin D. Roosevelt, 1933 (1938), p. 11.

text: For as children tremble and fear everything in the blind darkness, so we in the light sometimes fear what is no more to be feared than the things children in the dark hold in terror and imagine will come true.
author: Lucretius
work: De Rerum Natura (On the Nature of Things)
citation: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura (On the Nature of Things), Book II, l. 87.

text: The only limit to our realization of tomorrow will be our doubts of today. Let us move forward with strong and active faith.
author: Franklin D. Roosevelt
citation: Franklin D. Roosevelt. The Public Papers and Addresses of Franklin D. Roosevelt, 1944–45 (1950), p. 616, which states: "This is the latest draft of the President's proposed speech [for Jefferson Day, April 13, 1945]. The last sentence [quoted above] was written into the typed draft in his own hand. The draft was not the final one; the preparation of the final draft was prevented by death."

text: Though I am always in haste, I am never in a hurry.
author: John Wesley
citation: John Wesley (1703–1791). Letter to a member of the Society, 10th December 1777, Select Letters (1837).

text: That perfect tranquillity of life, which is nowhere to be found but in retreat, a faithful friend and a good library.
author: Aphra Behn
citation: Aphra Behn, in The Wonders of Solitude, 21 December 2011, p. 53

text: Inside the word “emergency” is “emerge”; from an emergency new things come forth. The old certainties are crumbling fast, but danger and possibility are sisters.
author: Rebecca Solnit
citation: Hope in the Dark: The Untold History of People Power (2004) · p12

text:
Come calm content serene and sweet,
O gently guide my pilgrim feet
To find thy hermit cell.
author: Anna Letitia Barbauld
work: Dictionary of Burning Words of Brilliant Writers
citation: Anna Letitia Barbauld, p. 161.

text:
Move outside the tangle of fear-thinking.
Live in silence.
author: Rumi
citation: Rumi, The Essential Rumi (1995), "A Community of the Spirit" in Ch. 1 : The Tavern, p. 2, translated by Coleman Barks with John Moyne, A. J. Arberry and Reynold A. Nicholson. Barks does not speak or read Persian; his 'translations' are therefore technically paraphrases and have been criticised by many scholars. Barks bases his paraphrases entirely on other English translations of Rumi which include renderings by Moyne and Nicholson.

text: I long for the countryside. That’s where I get my calm and tranquillity - from being able to come and find a spot of green.
author: Emilia Clarke
citation: Emilia Clarke, in Year of the Dragon (May 2012)

text: Because things are the way they are, things will not stay the way they are.
author: Bertolt Brecht
citation: Bertolt Brecht, as quoted in Dictionary of Contemporary Quotations (1976) by John Gordon Burke and Ned Kehde, p. 224, also in The Book of Positive Quotations (2007) by John Cook, p. 390

text: To me, fearless is not the absence of fear. It’s not being completely unafraid. To me, fearless is having fears. Fearless is having doubts. Lots of them. To me, fearless is living in spite of those things that scare you to death.
author: Taylor Swift
citation: Taylor Swift, on the liner notes on her Fearless album in 2008

text: We should never despair, our Situation before has been unpromising and has changed for the better, so I trust, it will again. If new difficulties arise, we must only put forth New Exertions and proportion our Efforts to the exigency of the times.
author: George Washington
citation: George Washington, letter to Major General Philip Schuyler, July 15, 1777.—The Writings of George Washington, ed. John C. Fitzpatrick, vol. 8, p. 408 (1933). This letter concerns the loss of Fort Ticonderoga.

text: When we long for life without difficulties, remind us that oaks grow strong in contrary winds and diamonds are made under pressure.
author: Peter Marshall
citation: Peter Marshall

text: There is the greatest practical benefit in making a few failures early in life.
author: Thomas Henry Huxley
citation: Thomas Henry Huxley, "On Medical Education (An Address to the Students of the Faculty of Medicine in University College, London, 1870)", in Critiques and Addresses (London: Macmillan and Co., 1873), p. 58.

text: The major work of the world is not done by geniuses. It is done by ordinary people, with balance in their lives, who have learned to work in an extraordinary manner.
author: Gordon B. Hinckley
citation: Gordon B. Hinckley, quoted by Michael Thomas Sunnarborg in 21 Keys to Work/Life Balance: Unlock Your Full Potential p. 51.

text: But failure has to be an option.
author: James Cameron
citation: James Cameron, Address to the 2010 TED conference (13 February 2010).

text: All beginnings are very troublesome things.
author: Letitia Elizabeth Landon
work: The History of Mabel Dacre’s First Lessons
citation: Letitia Elizabeth Landon, Traits and Trials of Early Life (1836), The History of Mabel Dacre's First Lessons.

text: Mindfulness is present-moment awareness. It takes place in the here and now. It is the observance of what is happening right now, in the present. It stays forever in the present, perpetually on the crest of the ongoing wave of passing time.
author: Henepola Gunaratana
citation: Henepola Gunaratana, Mindfulness in Plain English (2011), p. 134

text:
For solitude sometimes is best society,
And short retirement urges sweet return.
author: John Milton
citation: John Milton, Paradise Lost (1667; 1674), Book IX, line 249

text: If you aren’t in the moment, you are either looking forward to uncertainty, or back to pain and regret.
author: Jim Carrey
citation: Jim Carrey, in "Carrey: 'Life Is Too Beautiful': Star Talks About Bouts With Depression And His Spirituality" 60 Minutes (21 November 2004).

text: Light is the task when many share the toil.
author: Homer
citation: Homer, The Iliad, Book XII, line 493. Bryant's translation.

text:
The world goes up and the world goes down.
And the sunshine follows the rain;
And yesterday’s sneer and yesterday’s frown
Can never come over again.
author: Charles Kingsley
citation: Charles Kingsley, Songs, II. in Hoyt's New Cyclopedia Of Practical Quotations (1922), p. 93-96

text: We learn wisdom from failure much more than from success. We often discover what will do by finding out what will not do; and probably he who never made a mistake never made a discovery.
author: Samuel Smiles
citation: Samuel Smiles, Self-Help; with Illustrations of Character and Conduct, Ch. XI : Self-Culture — Facilities and Difficulties (1859).

text: Any time I make a record it’s followed by a painting period. It’s good crop rotation.
author: Joni Mitchell
work: Woman of Heart and Mind: A Life Story
citation: Woman of Heart and Mind: A Life Story (2003)

text: ‘Tis the gift to be simple, ‘tis the gift to be free.
author: Joseph Brackett
citation: Joseph Brackett, Simple Gifts (1848).

text: There is a budding morrow in midnight.
author: John Keats
citation: John Keats, Sonnet, Standing alone in giant Ignorance

text: The only way to make sense out of change is to plunge into it, move with it, and join the dance.
author: Alan Watts
citation: Alan Watts, The Wisdom of Insecurity (1951)

text: Ambition is the grand enemy of all peace.
author: John Cowper Powys
citation: John Cowper Powys, The Meaning of Culture (1929)

text: Humor is perhaps a sense of intellectual perspective: an awareness that some things are really important, others not; and that the two kinds are most oddly jumbled in everyday affairs.
author: Christopher Morley
citation: Christopher Morley, as quoted in An Enchanted Life : An Adept's Guide to Masterful Magick‎ (2001) by Patricia Telesco, p. 189

text: Even in the harshest places there is still wonder and beauty. Times are tough, but never forget the awe and majesty of life on this strange blue planet.
author: Rebecca Helm
citation: Rebecca Helm, in a Twitter post, quoted in Newly discovered 'glitter worms' dance and fight one another underwater (May 14, 2020) by Bonnie Burton, CNET

text:
Worthy books
Are not companions—they are solitudes:
We lose ourselves in them and all our cares.
author: Philip James Bailey
citation: Philip James Bailey, Festus (1813), scene A Village Feast. Evening.

text:
A late lark twitters from the quiet skies:
And from the west,
Where the sun, his day’s work ended,
Lingers as in content,
There falls on the old, gray city
An influence luminous and serene,
A shining peace.
author: William Ernest Henley
citation: William Ernest Henley, "Margaritæ Sorori", st. 1

text: You have to laugh at the things that hurt you just to keep yourself in balance, just to keep the world from running you plumb crazy.
author: Ken Kesey
work: One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest
citation: Ken Kesey, in One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest (1962)

text: The timeless in you is aware of life’s timelessness, And knows that yesterday is but today’s memory and tomorrow is today’s dream.
author: Khalil Gibran
citation: Khalil Gibran, in The Prophet,(1923)

text:
Now all the tree-tops lay asleep,
Like green waves on the sea,
As still as in the silent deep
The ocean-woods may be.
author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
citation: Percy Bysshe Shelley, The Recollection, II.

text: There are two things to aim at in life: first, to get what you want; and, after that, to enjoy it. Only the wisest of mankind achieve the second.
author: Logan Pearsall Smith
citation: Logan Pearsall Smith, Afterthoughts (1931), 'Life and Human Nature'.

text: A man is a small thing and the night is very large and full of wonders.
author: Lord Dunsany
citation: Lord Dunsany, The Laughter of the Gods, Act II, in Plays of Gods and Men (Boston: John W. Luce & Company, 1917), p. 102

text: The longest day at last bends down to evening.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
work: Wilhelm Meister’s Travels; or, The Renunciants
citation: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, Wilhelm Meister's Travels; or, The Renunciants (1821), tr. Thomas Carlyle (1821)

text: Where would there be leather enough to cover the entire world? With just the leather of my sandals, it is as if the whole world were covered. Likewise, I am unable to restrain external phenomena, but I shall restrain my own mind. What need is there to restrain anything else?
author: Santideva
work: A Guide to the Bodhisattva Way of Life
citation: Santideva, A Guide to the Bodhisattva Way of Life, V. Wallace and B. Wallace, trans. (1997), § 5.13.

text: Although men are accused of not knowing their own weakness, yet perhaps as few know their own strength. It is in men as in soils, where sometimes there is a vein of gold, which the owner knows not of.
author: Jonathan Swift
work: Thoughts on Various Subjects from Miscellanies
citation: Jonathan Swift,Thoughts on Various Subjects from Miscellanies (1711-1726).

text: I fear the popular notion of success stands in direct opposition in all points to the real and wholesome success.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: Ralph Waldo Emerson (1803–1882), American writer. 'Success', Society and Solitude (1870)

text:
Life is mostly froth and bubble;
Two things stand like stone:
Kindness in another’s trouble
Courage in our own.
author: Adam Lindsay Gordon
citation: Adam Lindsay Gordon, Ye Weary Wayfarer, Finis Exoptatus.

text: There never was night that had no morn.
author: Dinah Craik
citation: Dinah Craik, "The Golden Gate", refrain; Thirty Years (1881), p. 317

text:
Beneath a shivering canopy reclined,
Of aspen leaves that wave without a wind,
I love to lie, when lulling breezes stir
The spiry cones that tremble on the fir.
author: John Leyden
citation: John Leyden, Noontide.

text:
Under the greenwood tree
Who loves to lie with me,
And tune his merry note
Unto the sweet bird’s throat,
Come hither, come hither, come hither:
No enemy here shall he see,
But winter and rough weather.
author: William Shakespeare
citation: William Shakespeare, As You Like It (c.1599-1600), Act II, scene 5, line 1.

text: Because your own strength is unequal to the task, do not assume that it is beyond the powers of man; but if anything is within the powers and province of man, believe that it is within your own compass also.
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, VI, 19, as translated by Gerald H. Rendall, Marcus Aurelius Antoninus to Himself (1901), p. 66

text: If we can’t have sanity, we can fake it with humor. Humor gives you the same distance from the situation, the same metaview, only laughing is easier than sanity and possibly more fun.
author: Jude Milhon
citation: Jude Milhon, attributed via Usenet

text: In these troubled times it is a wholesome and necessary thing for us to turn again to the earth and in the contemplation of her beauties to know the sense of wonder and humility.
author: Rachel Carson
citation: Rachel Carson "The Exceeding Beauty of the World" (Words to Live by), This Week (1952), quoted in Karen F. Stein, Rachel Carson: Challenging Authors (Rotterdam: Sense Publishers, 2012), p. 54.

text:
In the dark I rest,
unready for the light which dawns
day after day,
eager to be shared.
Black silk, shelter me.
I need
more of the night before I open
eyes and heart
to illumination. I must still
grow in the dark like a root
not ready, not ready at all.
author: Denise Levertov
citation: Denise Levertov, "Eye Mask"; Evening Train (1992)

text: There are three things which are real: God, human folly, and laughter. Since the first two pass our comprehension, we must do what we can with the third.
author: Aubrey Menen
citation:
Aubrey Menen, Rama Retold (1954), p. 231. This is a modern retelling of part of the Ramayana. President John F. Kennedy presented his friend, White House appointment secretary David Powers, with a silver beer mug for his birthday, April 26, 1963. The inscription on the mug was a slight variation on the lines above:
There are three things which are real:

text: It’s no use crying over spilt evils. It’s better to mop them up laughing.
author: Eleanor Farjeon
citation: Eleanor Farjeon, in Gypsy and Ginger (1920)

text: He will through life be master of himself and a happy man who from day to day can have said, “I have lived: tomorrow the Father may fill the sky with black clouds or with cloudless sunshine.”
author: Horace
citation: Horace, Odes, Book III, ode xxix, line 41 (c. 23 BC and 13 BC)

text: Night was come, and her planets were risen: a safe, still night: too serene for the companionship of fear.
author: Charlotte Brontë
citation: Charlotte Brontë, Jane Eyre (1847), ch. 28

text: This was not judgement day — only morning. Morning: excellent and fair.
author: William Styron
citation: William Styron, Sophie's Choice (1979)

text:
One is nearer God’s heart in a garden
Than anywhere else on earth.
author: Dorothy Frances Gurney
citation: Dorothy Frances Gurney, God's Garden.

text: It is not so much for its beauty that the forest makes a claim upon men’s hearts, as for that subtle something, that quality of air that emanates from old trees, that so wonderfully changes and renews a weary spirit.
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
work: The Works of Robert Louis Stevenson
citation: Robert Louis Stevenson, in "Forest Notes" (1875-1876) "Morality" also in The Works of Robert Louis Stevenson, Vol. IX : Essays and Reviews (1906) edited by Charles Curis Bigelow and Temple Scott, p. 133.

text: I have seen the sea lashed into fury and tossed into spray, and its grandeur moves the soul of the dullest man; but I remember that it is not the billows, but the calm level of the sea from which all heights and depths are measured.
author: James A. Garfield
citation: James A. Garfield, speech nominating John Sherman for president; Proceedings of the Republican National Convention, Chicago, Illinois, June 2–8, 1880 (1881), p. 184. Garfield himself was ultimately nominated at this convention.

text:
To look up and not down,
To look forward and not back,
To look out and not in—and
To lend a hand.
author: Edward Everett Hale
citation: Edward Everett Hale, Rule of the "Harry Wadsworth Club", from Ten Times One is Ten (1870), Chapter IV

text: The delight of opening a new pursuit, or a new course of reading, imparts the vivacity and novelty of youth even to old age.
author: Isaac D'Israeli
work: Literary Character of Men of Genius
citation: Isaac D'Israeli, Literary Character of Men of Genius, Chapter XXII.

text: Decisions made against the will of the heart never bring good to anyone. Refusing may bring pain for a while, just for a moment, but agreeing to something merely to please someone aches forever and hurts everyone.
author: Sanu Sharma
citation: Sanu Sharma, Jigree

text:
Here are cool mosses deep,
And thro’ the moss the ivies creep,
And in the stream the long-leaved flowers weep,
And from the craggy ledge the poppy hangs in sleep.
author: Alfred Tennyson
citation: Alfred Tennyson, The Lotos-Eaters, Choric Song, Part I.

text: Not all those who wander are lost.
author: J.R.R. Tolkien
citation: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Fellowship of the Ring

text: Try to learn to breathe deeply, really to taste food when you eat, and when you sleep really to sleep. Try as much as possible to be wholly alive with all your might, and when you laugh, laugh like hell.
author: William Saroyan
work: The Daring Young Man on the Flying Trapeze
citation: William Saroyan, in The Daring Young Man on the Flying Trapeze (1934), Preface

text: Perplexity is the beginning of knowledge.
author: Khalil Gibran
citation: Khalil Gibran, The Voice of the Master, trans. Anthony R. Ferris (1958), p. 87.

text:
When the shore is won at last,
Who will count the billows past?
author: John Keble
citation: John Keble, Christian Year, Stanza John the Evangelist's Day, Stanza 5

text: Growth is an erratic forward movement: two steps forward, one step back. Remember that and be very gentle with yourself.
author: Julia Cameron
citation: Julia Cameron, The Artist's Way (1992).

text:
Life let us cherish, while yet the taper glows,
And the fresh flow’ret pluck ere it close;
Why are we fond of toil and care?
Why choose the rankling thorn to wear?
author: J. M. Usteri
citation: J. M. Usteri, Life let us Cherish.

text: Even on the most exalted throne in the world we are only sitting on our own bottom.
author: Michel de Montaigne
work: The Essays of Michel de Montaigne
citation: Michel de Montaigne, The Essays of Michel de Montaigne (1580), as translated by Jacob Zeitlin, vol. 3, p. 317 (1936); the translation of "Et au plus eslevé throne du monde, si ne sommes assis que sus nôstre cul" varies in other editions.

text:
How sweet the moonlight sleeps upon this bank!
Here will we sit and let the sounds of music
Creep in our ears: soft stillness, and the night
Becomes the touches of sweet harmony.
author: William Shakespeare
citation: William Shakespeare, The Merchant of Venice (late 1590s), Act V, scene 1, line 54.

text:
Since the bounty of Providence is new every day,
As we journey through life let us live by the way.
author: Walter Watson
citation: Walter Watson, Drinking Song.

text:
Welcome, ye shades! ye bowery Thickets hail!
Ye lofty Pines! ye venerable Oaks!
Ye Ashes wild, resounding o’er the steep!
Delicious is your shelter to the soul.
author: James Thomson
citation: James Thomson, The Seasons, Summer (1727), line 469.

text:
A man’s best things are nearest him,
Lie close about his feet.
author: Richard Monckton Milnes
citation: Richard Monckton Milnes (Lord Houghton), The Men of Old, Stanza 7.

text: It’s hard to see the forest when you’re a tree.
author: Paula Gunn Allen
citation: Paula Gunn Allen, Chapter Three

text:
When on the breath of Autumn’s breeze,
From pastures dry and brown,
Goes floating, like an idle thought,
The fair, white thistle-down;
O, then what joy to walk at will,
Upon the golden harvest-hill!
author: Mary Howitt
citation: Mary Howitt, Corn-Fields; reported in Hoyt's New Cyclopedia Of Practical Quotations (1922), p. 787.

text:
Gold that buys health can never be ill spent,
Nor hours laid out in harmless merriment.
author: John Webster
citation: John Webster, Westward Ho, Act V, scene 3, line 345.

text: Most people would succeed in small things, if they were not troubled with great ambitions.
author: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
citation: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, Drift-Wood, Table-Talk (1857)

text: Were I to live my life over again, I should live it just as I have done. I neither complain of the past, nor do I fear the future.
author: Michel de Montaigne
citation: Michel de Montaigne, Essays, On Repentance, Book III, Chapter II.

text: Life is like a game of tables, the chances are not in our power, but the playing is.
author: Terence
citation: Terence, Adelphi; also Plato, Commonwealth. Quoted by Jeremy Taylor, Holy Living, Section VI. Of Contentedness.

text:
The virtue lies
In the struggle, not the prize.
author: Richard Monckton Milnes
citation: Richard Monckton Milnes (Lord Houghton), The World to the Soul, 9. 1

text: The person attempting to travel two roads at once will get nowhere.
author: Xun Zi
work: Iron Sharpens Iron: Wisdom of the Ages
citation: Xun Zi quoted in: Errick A. Ford (2010) Iron Sharpens Iron: Wisdom of the Ages, p. 48.

text:
Slow buds the pink dawn like a rose
From out night’s gray and cloudy sheath;
Softly and still it grows and grows,
Petal by petal, leaf by leaf.
author: Susan Coolidge
citation: Susan Coolidge, "The Morning Comes Before the Sun", Verses (1880), p. 64

text: Men must be decided on what they will NOT do, and then they are able to act with vigor in what they ought to do.
author: Mencius
citation: Mencius, Works, Book IV, Part II, Chapter VIII

text:
Come, drink the mystic wine of Night,
Brimming with silence and the stars;
While earth, bathed in this holy light,
Is seen without its scars.
author: Louis Untermeyer
citation: Louis Untermeyer, "The Wine of Night", l. 1; Challenge (1914), p. 74

text:
The summer demands and takes away too much.
But night, the reserved, the reticent, gives more than it takes.
author: John Ashbery
citation: John Ashbery, "As One Put Drunk into a Packet-Boat"; Self-Portrait in a Convex Mirror (1975)

text: Nor on one string are all life’s jewels strung.
author: William Morris
citation: William Morris, Life and Death of Jason, Book 17, line 1,170.

text: A fresh mind keeps the body fresh. Take in the ideas of the day, drain off those of yesterday. As to the morrow, time enough to consider it when it becomes to-day.
author: Edward Bulwer-Lytton
work: Kenelm Chillingly: His Adventures and Opinions
citation: Edward Bulwer-Lytton, Kenelm Chillingly : His Adventures and Opinions (1873), Book I, Ch. 8

text: Many a genius has been slow of growth. Oaks that flourish for a thousand years do not spring up into beauty like a reed.
author: George Henry Lewes
citation: George Henry Lewes, The Spanish Drama, ch. 2 (1846).

text: Arts and sciences are not cast in a mould, but are found and perfected by degrees, by often handling and polishing, as bears leisurely lick their cubs into shape.
author: Michel de Montaigne
citation: Michel de Montaigne, Apology for Raimond Sebond, Book II, Chapter XII.

text: The fullness of life is in the hazards of life. And, at the worst, there is that in us which can turn defeat into victory.
author: Edith Hamilton
work: The Great Age of Greek Literature
citation: Edith Hamilton, The Great Age of Greek Literature (1942), p. 243. She was referring to Aeschylus.

text:
Music that gentlier on the spirit lies
Than tir’d eyelids upon tir’d eyes.
author: Alfred Tennyson
citation: Alfred Tennyson, The Lotos Eaters, Choric Song, Stanza 1.

text: You cannot force ideas. Successful ideas are the result of slow growth. Ideas do not reach perfection in a day, no matter how much study is put upon them.
author: Alexander Graham Bell
citation: Alexander Graham Bell, Bell Telephone Talk, Interview with Bell published in How They Succeeded (1901) by Orison Swett Marden, Ch. 2. (1901).

text:
A little rain will fill
The lily’s cup which hardly moists the field.
author: Edwin Arnold
citation: Edwin Arnold, The Light of Asia (1879), Book VI, line 215

text: The longest way must have its close,—the gloomiest night will wear on to a morning.
author: Harriet Beecher Stowe
citation: Harriet Beecher Stowe, Uncle Tom's Cabin (1852), vol. 2, ch. 40

text: When anxious, uneasy and bad thoughts come, I go to the sea, and the sea drowns them out with its great wide sounds, cleanses me with its noise and imposes a rhythm upon everything in me that is bewildered and confused.
author: Rainer Maria Rilke
citation: Rainer Maria Rilke, Letters of Rainer Maria Rilke 1892-1910. Also quoted in Murphy, Edward F., The Crown Treasury of Relevant Quotations, New York : Crown Publishers, 1978 (pg. 517).

text: The one who knows he is confused is not that confused.
author: Zhuangzi
citation: Zhuangzi, The Book of Chuang Tzu, as translated by M. Palmer, et. al. (Penguin: 1996), p. 103

text: Charging back and forth isn’t progress. Small but steady forward motion is.
author: Algis Budrys
citation: Algis Budrys, On Clouds of Glory in Astounding, July 1955, p. 32

text: Personally the books by which I have profited infinitely more than by any others have been those in which profit was a by-product of the pleasure; that is, I read them because I enjoyed them, because I liked reading them, and the profit came in as part of the enjoyment.
author: Theodore Roosevelt
citation: Theodore Roosevelt, (reprint of 1913 1st edition)

text: I don’t think necessity is the mother of invention — invention, in my opinion, arises directly from idleness, possibly also from laziness. To save oneself trouble.
author: Agatha Christie
citation: Agatha Christie, An Autobiography (1977)

text: There ought to be a place for people without ambition, I mean a better place than the one usually reserved.
author: Charles Bukowski
citation: Charles Bukowski, Factotum (1975)

text: To endure is greater than to dare; to tire out hostile fortune; to be daunted by no difficulty; to keep heart when all have lost it; to go through intrigue spotless; and to forgo even ambition when the end is gained — who can say this is not greatness?
author: William Makepeace Thackeray
citation: William Makepeace Thackeray, The Virginians (1857-1859), Chapter 92

text:
How beautiful is night!
A dewy freshness fills the silent air;
No mist obscures, nor cloud nor speck nor stain
Breaks the serene of heaven.
author: Robert Southey
citation: Robert Southey, Thalaba (1800), bk. I

text:
Night is the time for rest;
How sweet, when labours close,
To gather round an aching breast
The curtain of repose,
Stretch the tired limbs, and lay the head
Down on our own delightful bed!
author: James Montgomery
citation: James Montgomery, "Night", st. 1; Forget Me Not for 1824 (1823), p. 179

text: We think a happy life consists in tranquility of mind.
author: Cicero
citation: Cicero, De Natura Deorum – On the Nature of the Gods (45 BC)

text: Comedy is a weird but very beautiful thing. Even though it seems foolish and silly and crazy, comedy has the most to say about the human condition. Because if you can laugh, you can get by. You can survive when things are bad when you have a sense of humor.
author: Mel Brooks
citation: Mel Brooks, All About Me! (New York: Ballantine Books, 2021), p. 451

text:
Down the hill I went, and then,
I forgot the ways of men,
For night-scents, heady and damp and cool
Wakened ecstasy in me
On the brink of a shining pool.
author: Sara Teasdale
citation: Sara Teasdale, "August Moonrise"; Flame and Shadow (1920)

text:
Life, believe, is not a dream,
So dark as sages say;
Oft a little morning rain
Foretells a pleasant day!
author: Charlotte Brontë
citation: Charlotte Brontë, Life.
